## "For God's Sake Hold Your Tongue": Colloquial Imperative and the Defence of Private Love

John Donne's "The Canonization" opens not with the elevated invocation of classical epic or the refined melancholy of Petrarchan longing, but with a blunt, exasperated imperative that sounds more like dramatic speech than lyric ornament:

Composed during Donne's years as a law student and aspiring courtier, before his ordination in 1615 transformed him into Dean of St Paul's, this poem belongs to the period of his most audacious secular lyrics. The biographical context is inseparable from its rhetoric: Donne's secret marriage to Anne More in 1601 forfeited Sir Thomas Egerton's patronage, condemned the couple to years of financial hardship, and supplied the worldly critics whose censure the speaker deflects. The opening stanza's strategy is brilliantly concessive. The speaker invites detractors to mock his age, illness, and poverty, to pursue wealth, office, court favour, or even numismatic contemplation of the king's coinage, anything, provided they "let me love." The repeated conditional "So you will let me love" transforms erotic privacy into a rights claim, establishing the central conflict between passionate inwardness and public duty that structures Jacobean Metaphysical poetry.

The stanza form, five nine-line stanzas rhyming ABBACCCDD, permits sustained development of each argumentative movement while the closing couplet (lines 8–9) delivers epigrammatic resolution. For UGC NET English candidates, the opening's colloquial energy exemplifies what T. S. Eliot later identifies as Metaphysical poetry's "unified sensibility": the capacity to fuse thought and feeling, sacred and profane registers, within a single linguistic gesture.
## Alas, Alas: The Harmlessness of Sighs and the Insulation of Desire
The second stanza shifts from dismissal to forensic defence, asking who suffers injury from the lovers' private passion:

The rhetorical questions construct love as a victimless experience insulated from public consequence. Sighs do not drown merchant ships; tears do not flood neighbours' fields; the lover's colds do not delay spring; his fevers do not swell plague mortality lists. Meanwhile, soldiers discover wars and lawyers discover lawsuits regardless of the lovers' devotion. The concluding line, "Though she and I do love", rhymes with public quarrels only to emphasise love's irrelevance to them. Donne's argumentative logic anticipates liberal defences of private life, yet the stanza's irony is double-edged: the speaker protests too much, and the poem's later stanzas will reveal love's capacity to "contract" the whole world's soul into the lovers' eyes. Harmlessness is a rhetorical opening position, not the poem's final truth.

For historicist criticism, this stanza engages early Stuart England's intensifying debates about the proper scope of secular love poetry. Puritan moralism, court scandal, and religious controversy made Donne's erotic lyrics simultaneously thrilling and dangerous. The speaker's defence does not appeal to theological sanction but to empirical absence of damage, a modern-sounding argument that Metaphysical wit renders through hyperbolic negation.

> Alas! alas! who's injured by my love?  
> What merchant's ships have my sighs drown'd?  
> Who says my tears have overflow'd his ground?  
> When did my colds a forward spring remove?  
> When did the heats which my veins fill  
> Add one more to the plaguy bill?  
> Soldiers find wars, and lawyers find out still  
> Litigious men, which quarrels move,  
> Though she and I do love.  
> (Grierson, ed., "The Canonization", ll. 10–18)
## Flies, Tapers, Phoenix: The Metaphysical Conceit and the Unity of Opposites
Stanza III escalates from logical defence to transformative conceit, yoking heterogeneous objects through intellectual aggression rather than sensuous description:

The lovers become flies, candles that consume themselves, eagle and dove fused in a single being, and finally the phoenix, mythical bird that dies and rises from its own ashes. The claim "we two being one, are it" asserts that the couple embodies the phoenix riddle, solving through erotic union the paradox of simultaneous death and renewal. Donne's conceit draws on Renaissance Neoplatonism and hermetic traditions that fuse opposites into unity: male and female, sacred and profane, life and death coalesce in "one neutral thing." The stanza's closing "Mysterious by this love" imports theological vocabulary, mystery in the sacramental sense, into profane experience, preparing the sacred-profane fusion that culminates in the title conceit.

A. J. Smith's work on Metaphysical wit emphasises that such comparisons do both decorate and argue. Each image advances a claim about love's transformative power. Flies suggest triviality and mortality; tapers suggest self-sacrificing illumination; eagle and dove combine strength and gentleness; the phoenix encodes resurrection. The stanza form's sustained nine lines allows each conceit to develop before the couplet resolves it into mystery, a formal enactment of the intellectual labour Metaphysical poetry demands from its readers.

> Call us what you will, we are made such by love;  
> Call her one, me another fly,  
> We're tapers too, and at our own cost die,  
> And we in us find the eagle and the dove,  
> The phoenix riddle hath more wit  
> By us; we two being one, are it.  
> So, to one neutral thing both sexes fit.  
> We die and rise the same, and prove  
> Mysterious by this love.  
> (Grierson, ed., "The Canonization", ll. 19–27)
## Canonized for Love: Verse as Martyrology and Sacred Tomb
The fourth stanza introduces the poem's titular conceit, proposing that if the lovers are unfit for conventional burial, they will be "canonized for love" through literary transmission:

Donne systematically imports religious vocabulary, "canonized," "hymns," "ashes", into erotic context. Sonnets become "pretty rooms," compact architectural spaces that house the lovers' legend as effectively as elaborate tombs house mortal remains. The well-wrought urn, evoking classical funeral vessels, suggests that lyric form itself is sacred monument. The process of canonization, in Roman Catholic martyrology, examines saints' lives for evidence of holiness; Donne ironically applies this scrutiny to profane lovers whose "legend" will be preserved in verse. The parallel with Spenser's Sonnet 75 ("My verse your virtues rare shall eternize") and Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 ("So long lives this, and this gives life to thee") situates Donne within the English tradition of poetic immortality, yet his tone is provocatively blasphemous where Spenser is earnest and Shakespeare is ambiguous.

John Carey's biographical criticism links the canonization conceit to Donne's personal experience of social disgrace after his marriage to Anne More. Excluded from court preferment, financially strained, physically marked by illness, Donne reimagines worldly failure as sainthood. Love becomes the medium of apotheosis, and poetry the instrument of martyrological record. The sacred-profane tension, are we witnessing heterodox devotion or playful blasphemy?, remains among the poem's most productive critical disputes.
## Future Lovers and the Devotional Afterlife of the Lyric
The final stanza projects the lovers into a future in which they are venerated as patron saints of erotic devotion:

Future lovers will "invoke" the speaker and his beloved as intercessors, begging from heaven "a pattern" of the love that made the pair each other's "hermitage"—sacred retreat. The lovers' eyes become mirrors and spies that "epitomize" the world, contracting all geography and polity into a single erotic focus. The stanza transforms private passion into universal exemplarity: countries, towns, and courts petition the canonized lovers for devotional models. The poem thus anticipates its own posterity as literature of veneration, completing the canonization it proclaims.

The closing image reverses stanza II's claim of public harmlessness. Love here is not insulated from the world but capable of reconstituting it entirely within the lovers' gaze. The progression from "let me love" to "invoke us" traces an arc from defensive privacy to public sainthood, from exasperated imperative to liturgical invocation. Donne's lyric becomes both the record and the instrument of apotheosis.
## Eliot, Johnson, and the Canonization of Donne

The reception of "The Canonization" mirrors its thematic concern with literary immortality. Donne's lyrics circulated in manuscript among a coterie audience during his lifetime; the 1633 posthumous edition edited by his son established the text for subsequent tradition. Seventeenth-century admirers including George Herbert, Richard Crashaw, Henry Vaughan, and Andrew Marvell inherit Donne's intellectual conceits and sacred-profane diction. Augustan critics find his wit strained and his metrics harsh: Samuel Johnson's account of Metaphysical "discordia concors"—yoking heterogeneous ideas by violence, captures both admiration and unease. The Romantic revival led by Coleridge and Browning, and T. S. Eliot's 1921 essay "The Metaphysical Poets," restore Donne to the centre of the English canon, praising the unified sensibility that "The Canonization" exemplifies.

Modern criticism emphasises the poem's gender politics, religious irony, and anticipation of desire as self-constituting identity. Whether "For God's sake" opens with genuine piety or ironic exasperation; whether the beloved is Anne More or an earlier lover; whether canonization subverts or reinforces patriarchal ideals, these disputed questions sustain the poem's analytical richness. For comparative study, "The Canonization" stands at the intersection of Petrarchan praise, Horatian monument, and Counter-Reformation martyrology, transformed by Donne's Jacobean wit into a manifesto declaring that erotic devotion constitutes a holiness worthy of verse.

In five stanzas of mounting rhetorical complexity, Donne conducts us from colloquial impatience through logical defence, metaphysical transformation, literary canonization, and liturgical projection. "The Canonization" remains the definitive expression of Metaphysical love poetry's audacity: the claim that to love passionately, in defiance of worldly censure, is to become what the world will later worship as sacred exemplar. The poem does more than describe that apotheosis; by surviving four centuries of critical invocation, it enacts it.

John Donne (1572–1631)
Original title: "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning" (from *Songs and Sonnets*)
c. 1611 (first published 1633) · Early Modern English · Jacobean England; metaphysical poetry · Jacobean Era · Metaphysical lyric in nine quatrains of iambic tetrameter (ABAB rhyme)
## The Geometry of a Parting That Must Not Grieve

At the centre of "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning" lies a rhetorical paradox that defines the metaphysical love lyric at its most intellectually ambitious: the speaker insists that true love requires the suppression of mourning precisely at the moment when physical separation makes grief most natural. Composed around 1611, when Donne accompanied Sir Robert Drury on a diplomatic mission to France and left his wife Anne behind in England, the poem addresses a beloved who remains unnamed in the text but is traditionally identified with Anne Donne. The occasion is practical and prosaic, months of aristocratic travel across the Channel, yet the poem converts that worldly departure into a sustained philosophical argument about the nature of union, absence, and spiritual fidelity. Where a conventional valediction might license tears, sighs, and public display, Donne's speaker forbids them outright, proposing instead that the lovers' bond is of such refinement that outward grief would profane rather than honour it.

The poem's opening movement establishes this prohibition through a sequence of analogies that elevate the lovers above the common run of parting lovers. The speaker compares their separation to the quiet death of virtuous men, whose souls pass so gently that friends dispute whether they are still alive, and then to the silent melting of gold, which loses nothing of its substance as it is drawn into finer form:

The diction here is characteristically Donnean in its fusion of the sacred and the sensual. "Profanation" imports a theological register into the domain of erotic joy, suggesting that the lovers' intimacy possesses a sacramental quality that public lament would violate. The "laity"—those outside the consecrated circle of the relationship, are not entitled to witness or interpret this love. Mourning, in this formulation, is more than indecorous; it is a category error, an attempt to measure a spiritual bond by the standards of corporeal attachment. The iambic tetrameter quatrains, with their alternating ABAB rhyme, create a measured, argumentative pace suited to persuasion rather than outcry. Each stanza advances a step in a dialectical ladder, refuting a lower form of love or grief before ascending to a higher plane.

> So let us melt, and make no noise,  
> No tear-floods, nor sigh-tempests move;  
> 'Twere profanation of our joys  
> To tell the laity our love.  
> (John Donne, *The Complete English Poems*, ed. A. J. Smith, ll. 5–8)
## Deathbeds, Earthquakes, and the Hierarchy of Motion

Donne's method in the first three stanzas is to establish a hierarchy of motion and disturbance that prepares the elevation of the lovers' bond above physical separation. The comparison to virtuous men dying quietly introduces a model of transition without trauma: the soul departs so subtly that the body seems unchanged, and friends must debate whether life has ended. This analogue suggests that the lovers' parting, too, should be imperceptible to external observers, an internal realignment rather than a visible rupture. The melting-gold image reinforces the point: gold does not vanish when heated; it changes state while retaining its essential nature. The lovers are asked to "melt" into one another without the acoustic violence of tears and sighs, which Donne figures as meteorological catastrophes, "tear-floods" and "sigh-tempests", that would disturb the atmosphere of their joy.
The third stanza introduces a cosmological analogue that is among the poem's most technically sophisticated moves:

Earthly tremors, earthquakes, cause alarm because they disrupt the sublunary world, the realm below the moon where change, decay, and sensory experience dominate. Celestial motion, by contrast, is vast yet harmless: the "trepidation of the spheres" refers to the pre-Copernican astronomical theory that the heavenly bodies tremble or vibrate in their orbits without causing terrestrial harm. Donne exploits this distinction to argue that the lovers' separation, like heavenly motion, may involve great distance without genuine injury. The inferior love that cannot endure absence is tied to the sublunary sphere; the refined love that the speaker claims operates on a celestial plane where movement does not imply dissolution. For UGC NET English candidates, this stanza exemplifies the metaphysical poet's habit of yoking heterogeneous domains, geology, astronomy, theology, and erotics, into a single argumentative structure.
## Dull Sublunary Love and the Mind's Assurance

Having established the cosmological framework, the poem turns to a direct contrast between inferior and superior forms of love. The fourth stanza defines the "dull sublunary lovers" whose attachment cannot survive absence:

The phrase "whose soul is sense" compresses a philosophical argument into four words. For these lovers, love is constituted entirely by sensory presence, touch, sight, proximity, and absence removes the very element that gave the love its being. Donne's syntax enacts the dependency it describes: the love "cannot admit / Of absence" because absence "doth remove / The thing which elemented it." The causal chain is tight and inexorable. This is love as appetite, love as habit, love as the comfort of physical nearness. It is, the speaker implies, the love of the "laity" condemned in stanza two, the love that requires public performance and collapses when the beloved is out of sight.

The fifth stanza pivots to the speaker's own bond, which is "so much refined" that it does not depend on "eyes, lips, and hands"—the instruments of sense. Instead, the lovers are "inter-assured of the mind," a phrase that locates the essence of their union in mutual consciousness rather than mutual presence. The word "inter-assured" suggests a reciprocal confidence, a knowledge held in common that does not require continual sensory confirmation. This is the Neoplatonic love tradition filtered through Donne's distinctive voice: love as the union of minds or souls, transcending the body's geography. Yet Donne does not abandon the body entirely. The poem's later stanzas will insist that the lovers are "two" as well as "one," and the famous compass conceit depends on a physical instrument whose two feet remain materially distinct even as they describe a single circle. The reconciliation of unity and duality is the poem's central metaphysical achievement.

> Dull sublunary lovers' love  
> —Whose soul is sense—cannot admit  
> Of absence, 'cause it doth remove  
> The thing which elemented it.  
> (John Donne, *The Complete English Poems*, ed. A. J. Smith, ll. 13–16)
## Gold Beaten Thin and the Twin Compasses
The sixth stanza articulates the poem's central thesis in one of Donne's most celebrated images:

The soul-union declared here is paradoxical from the outset: "two souls" that "are one." Physical separation is not a breach but an expansion, a word that reverses the expected emotional valence of parting. Where common sense associates absence with diminishment, Donne proposes that true union intensifies under separation, just as gold beaten thin covers more space without losing its substance. The metallurgical conceit draws on the artisanal knowledge of early modern England, where goldsmiths hammered precious metal into leaf so fine it could float on air. The image is simultaneously material and spiritual: the love is stretched, refined, extended across the distance between England and France, yet it remains gold, unchanged in essence, only altered in form.

This expansion prepares the introduction of the poem's most famous conceit, the twin compasses of the final three stanzas. If the lovers "be two, they are two so / As stiff twin compasses are two"—two legs joined at a single pivot, inseparable in function though distinct in motion. The beloved is the "fix'd foot," the stationary centre; the traveller is the moving foot that roams the circumference. Crucially, the fixed foot "leans and hearkens" after the roaming leg, and "grows erect" as the circle closes and the traveller returns. The geometry ensures that the journey ends where it began:

The compass image has become the standard reference point in discussions of metaphysical conceit in English poetry, celebrated by T. S. Eliot in "The Metaphysical Poets" (1921) as an instance of the unified sensibility that yokes disparate experience into a single thought. For examination purposes, candidates should note how the conceit operates on multiple levels: it is a mathematical instrument, a metaphor for marital fidelity, a diagram of spiritual unity within physical separation, and, controversially, a possible encoding of gendered hierarchy, with the wife assigned the passive, central role and the husband the active, itinerant one.

> Our two souls therefore, which are one,  
> Though I must go, endure not yet  
> A breach, but an expansion,  
> Like gold to airy thinness beat.  
> (John Donne, *The Complete English Poems*, ed. A. J. Smith, ll. 21–24)

> Thy firmness makes my circle just,  
> And makes me end where I begun.  
> (John Donne, *The Complete English Poems*, ed. A. J. Smith, ll. 35–36)
## Sacrament, Neoplatonism, and the Fixed Foot

The critical reception of "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning" has centred on three disputed questions that UGC NET syllabi regularly foreground. First, the identity of the addressee: Anne Donne is the traditional candidate, supported by biographical evidence of Donne's 1611 journey, but the poem's speaker never names the beloved, and the argument it constructs is philosophically general enough to transcend any single occasion. Second, the degree to which the poem encodes Christian sacramental marriage doctrine versus secular Neoplatonism: the language of profanation, the emphasis on soul-union, and the compass's insistence on return and closure resonate with contemporary theology of marriage as an indissoluble spiritual bond, yet the poem's intellectual apparatus draws equally on Ficino and the Platonic tradition of love as the soul's ascent toward the divine. Third, the gender politics of the compass conceit: feminist readings have questioned whether the assignment of the "fix'd foot" to the beloved reinscribes early modern patriarchal norms, while other critics argue that the fixed foot's agency, its leaning, hearkening, and final erectness, grants the stationary partner an active, sustaining role in the relationship's geometry.

What remains undisputed is the poem's formal mastery. Nine quatrains of iambic tetrameter, each advancing a single step in a cumulative argument, create a structure that is at once lyric and logical. The valediction genre typically licenses emotional extravagance; Donne inverts that convention, using the occasion of parting to define a love so refined that grief would be a misunderstanding. The poem's final line, "And makes me end where I begun", converts separation into completion, turning the traveller's arc into a perfect circle whose centre is the beloved's steadfastness. In this resolution, Donne achieves what Eliot identified as the hallmark of metaphysical poetry: the fusion of thought and feeling into a single complex response. "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning" is one of the supreme achievements of the Jacobean love lyric, a poem that transforms the pain of absence into a geometry of fidelity and returns.
George Herbert (1593–1633)
Original title: "The Altar" (from *The Temple*)
c. 1630–1633 (first published 1633) · Early Modern English · Caroline England; Anglican devotional verse · Caroline Era; metaphysical religious poetry · Pattern poem (shape poem / figured verse)
## The Broken Altar at the Threshold of the Temple

At the threshold of George Herbert's *The Temple*—the manuscript sequence of sacred poems arranged by the poet before his death and published posthumously in 1633, stands "The Altar," a lyric whose meaning is inseparable from its visual form. The poem constructs, through the length and centring of its lines, the silhouette of a church altar on the page: a broad base, a narrowing shaft, and a widening surface at the top. This typographical layout is not decorative embellishment; it is the poem's central argument made visible. Herbert asks us to see an altar while reading about consecration, uniting icon and text in a single devotional act. The speaker addresses God directly, "Lord, thy servant", and declares that he rears "a broken ALTAR" made of heart and tears, insisting that its parts were framed by divine hand alone:

The opening paradox is immediately striking. Altars are structures of sacrifice and offering, places where the human and divine meet in ritual exchange; yet this altar is "broken," assembled from the most unstable of materials, a living heart and falling tears, rather than from hewn stone or polished marble. The brokenness is not a defect to be repaired but the condition of authentic worship. Herbert's devotional persona offers not wholeness but fracture, not confidence but weeping, and in doing so aligns the poem with the Psalmist's declaration that God does not despise "a broken and a contrite heart" (Psalm 51:17). For UGC NET English candidates, "The Altar" exemplifies the metaphysical religious lyric at its most compressed: theological argument, biblical typology, and formal innovation fused into fourteen lines that function simultaneously as poem and visual emblem.

> A broken ALTAR, Lord, thy servant rears,  
> Made of a heart, and cemented with tears:  
> Whose parts are as thy hand did frame;  
> No workman's tool hath touch'd the same.  
> (George Herbert, *The English Poems of George Herbert*, ed. Helen Gardner, ll. 1–4)
## Pattern Poetry and the Visual Theology of Sacrifice

"The Altar" belongs to the tradition of *carmen figuratum*, pattern poetry whose shape on the page contributes to its signification. Classical precedents include Simias of Rhodes and the Latin poet Optatianus Porfyrius; in English, Herbert's own "Easter Wings"—printed on facing pages in the 1633 edition of *The Temple*—forms a pair of winged shapes that rise and fall with the poem's argument about resurrection. The 1633 typography, supervised by Nicholas Ferrar and the community at Little Gidding after Herbert's death, is integral to the poem's meaning. Modern editions that linearise the text, printing the lines as conventional left-aligned verse, strip the poem of a dimension that Herbert deliberately constructed. Critics debate whether contemporary reprints should preserve the shaped layout or prioritise readability, but the consensus in Herbert studies holds that the visual form is not optional: us who encounters "The Altar" only as a sequence of fourteen lines misses half the poem.

The pattern-poem tradition serves Herbert's broader project in *The Temple*: the human soul as a consecrated structure. The book's governing metaphor treats the self as a temple, a house of God that must be built, repaired, and offered through prayer, obedience, and sacrifice. "The Altar" announces this architecture at the sequence's opening, establishing the terms on which the subsequent lyrics will operate. The altar in Christian worship is the site of eucharistic sacrifice, the table where bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ; Herbert's poem transposes that liturgical object onto the believer's interior life. The heart becomes stone, the stone becomes altar, and the altar remains broken, never a monument of human achievement but a vessel of divine craftsmanship. This visual theology insists that worship is not performed through external grandeur but through the offering of a fractured self.
## Stone, Heart, and the Divine Mason
The poem's central narrowing, lines five through eight, which form the shaft of the altar shape, articulates the metaphysical fusion of heart and stone that drives Herbert's conceit:

The heart, in conventional lyric tradition, is the seat of feeling, passion, and vulnerability. Stone, by contrast, signifies hardness, endurance, and resistance to change. Herbert yokes these opposed properties into a single figure: the heart is stone, and only God's power can cut it. The divine mason replaces the human workman explicitly excluded in the opening stanza—"No workman's tool hath touch'd the same." This denial of human artisanal agency is theologically precise. In Reformation spirituality, salvation cannot be earned through human merit or craft; the broken heart is God's work alone, framed by divine hand, cut by divine power. The poem's visual narrowing enacts the cutting it describes: the lines grow shorter as they approach the centre, as though the stone heart were being shaped, reduced, refined to its essential form.

The stony heart also invokes biblical precedents. Ezekiel 36:26 promises that God will remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh; Herbert reverses the expected direction of transformation, beginning with stone and requiring divine intervention to shape it into something offerable. The flint and martyrdom imagery of the widening lines, "Such flints as these are, / Or stones that suffer martyrdom", connects the speaker's interior fracture to the witness of those who died for faith. Martyrdom stones are stones that have endured the ultimate test of hardness; the speaker's heart, similarly resistant, can only be offered if God first cuts and consecrates it.

> A HEART alone  
> Is such a stone,  
> As nothing but  
> Thy pow'r doth cut.  
> (George Herbert, *The English Poems of George Herbert*, ed. Helen Gardner, ll. 5–8)
## Martyrdom Stones and the Widening Petition
As the poem's lines widen again toward the altar's upper surface, the speaker petitions through the fractured heart's many corners:

The syntax distributes prayer across the heart's fragments: "each part" prays "in each corner," as though the brokenness of the altar multiplied the sites of devotion rather than diminishing them. Meekness, the virtue Herbert consistently privileges over eloquence or theological display, characterises these distributed prayers. The flints and martyrdom stones extend the stone imagery into a catalogue of hardness and sacrifice. Flint strikes fire; martyrdom stones bear witness under torture. Both figures suggest that the material resistant to human shaping becomes, under divine handling, the substance of offering.

The widening structure of these lines completes the visual altar: the poem's shape mirrors the ecclesiastical object it describes, with the broad base of lines one through four, the narrow shaft of lines five through eight, and the expanding surface of lines nine through fourteen. This convergence of form and content is what T. S. Eliot, in his essay on Herbert, identifies as the poet's achievement of a "plain style" that is never merely simple: the short words, direct address, and liturgical compression carry metaphysical paradox without ornate baroque elaboration. Where Donne's religious lyrics often dramatise spiritual crisis through violent paradox and colloquial energy, Herbert's devotional voice tends toward quiet insistence, the voice of the country parson Herbert became at Bemerton from 1630 until his death in 1633.

> Wherefore each part of my hard heart  
> Meekly in each corner prays:  
> Such flints as these are,  
> Or stones that suffer martyrdom.  
> (George Herbert, *The English Poems of George Herbert*, ed. Helen Gardner, ll. 9–12)
## From Contrite Heart to Consecrated Surface
The poem's closing lines resolve the pattern, completing the transformation from stone to heart to altar:

The temporal sequence, "alate" (lately, recently) cut to a heart, and "now" made an altar stone, charts a process of consecration that has already occurred within the poem's brief compass. The whole remains "little," a modest offering without grandeur, yet it has achieved the status of altar stone, fit for sacrifice. The final line's typography in the 1633 edition, with "ALTAR" in capitals echoing the opening "ALTAR," frames the poem as a completed structure: the broken altar reared in line one has become, by line fourteen, a consecrated surface. Image, layout, and doctrine arrive at the same point.

Critical debate surrounds the extent to which "The Altar" encodes Laudian altar theology, the High Church emphasis on eucharistic sacrifice and ceremonial worship associated with Archbishop Laud, or broadly Anglican symbolism compatible with the via media Herbert embodied. The poem's publication in 1633, during intensifying conflict over church ceremony, lends political resonance to its imagery, yet Herbert's devotional practice at Bemerton emphasised interior piety and pastoral duty rather than polemical sectarianism. The altar here is primarily metaphorical, the interior shrine of a soul that offers itself in brokenness rather than in triumph.

"The Altar" established English pattern poetry as a major mode of devotional expression. Its influence extends to later visual and concrete poetry, and it remains paired with Donne's *Holy Sonnets* in metaphysical anthologies as the supreme example of religious wit in shaped form. For us approaching *The Temple* for the first time, the poem functions as both threshold and key: it announces that the book's architecture will be visual as well as verbal, that sacrifice will be defined as spiritual fracture rather than material display, and that the God addressed is not a distant sovereign but a divine mason who alone can cut the stony heart into an altar fit for worship. In fourteen lines and a single silhouette, Herbert accomplishes what the entire sequence will elaborate: the consecration of the human soul as a house of prayer.

> The whole is little but a stone,  
> Cut to a HEART alate,  
> And now made a ALTAR stone.  
> (George Herbert, *The English Poems of George Herbert*, ed. Helen Gardner, ll. 13–14)
John Milton (1608–1674)
Original title: *Lycidas*

1637 (first published 1638) · Early Modern English (with Latin epigraph and pastoral conventions) · English pastoral elegy; Caroline Cambridge · Caroline Era; English Renaissance elegy · Pastoral elegy in irregular rhyming verse (193 lines)
## The Uncouth Swain and the Forced Harvest

At the heart of *Lycidas* lies a tension that defines the English pastoral elegy at its most ambitious: the poem mourns a specific, historical death, the drowning of Edward King, Milton's fellow student at Christ's College, Cambridge, on 10 August 1637, through the fictive machinery of Arcadian shepherds, classical rivers, and mythological figures. Composed in November 1637 and published in *Justa Edouardo King Naufrago* (Cambridge, 1638), the memorial volume of poems by Cambridge men, Milton's contribution closes the collection with a work that would become the supreme achievement of English pastoral elegy. The speaker is an "uncouth swain," a rustic shepherd whose very uncouthness, his lack of polish, his outsider status, signals the poem's self-conscious relation to pastoral convention. He opens by breaking the seasonal order of the pastoral world, plucking laurel and myrtle before their time:

The invocation is deliberately disruptive. Pastoral elegy traditionally aligns mourning with the cycle of nature, autumn leaves, winter frost, the ripeness of grief, but Milton's swain forces the harvest prematurely. "Forc'd fingers rude" shatter leaves "before the mellowing year," enacting at the level of diction and imagery the violence of Edward King's early death. The laurel and myrtle are the poet's traditional emblems: laurel for achievement and fame, myrtle for love and pastoral song. To pluck them crude and harsh is to declare that the poet's vocation has been interrupted before fulfilment. For UGC NET English candidates, this opening establishes the poem's central question: whether poetry and poetic ambition survive the poet's own premature death, a question that will reverberate through the Fame digression and the final consolation.

> Yet once more, O ye laurels, and once more  
> Ye myrtles brown, with ivy never sere,  
> I come to pluck your berries harsh and crude,  
> And, with forc'd fingers rude,  
> Shatter your leaves before the mellowing year.  
> (John Milton, *The Complete Shorter Poems*, ed. John Carey, ll. 1–5)
## Pastoral Convention and the Death of Edward King

Milton's choice of pastoral elegy for Edward King follows an established English precedent: Spenser's *Astrophel* (1595), composed for Sir Philip Sidney, provided the immediate model for commemorative pastoral collections that universalise private loss through Arcadian fiction. The classical lineage extends through Theocritus, Virgil's *Eclogue 10*, Bion, Moschus, and Ovid, whose shepherds, flowers, and lament structures inform Milton's machinery. Yet *Lycidas* is never merely imitative. The pastoral frame enables political and ecclesiastical critique that would be difficult to articulate in direct contemporary reference: the corrupt clergy condemned by St Peter, the "grim Wolf" that devours the flock, and the "two-handed engine" of apocalyptic judgment all operate within a fictive landscape that nonetheless engages Caroline debates over pastoral neglect, Laudian church politics, and the spiritual duties of the minister.

The elegiac narrative unfolds through a floral catalogue, primrose, violet, jasmine, crowflower, strewed by shepherd-poets who question the value of poetry in the face of early death. The poem widens from private grief to institutional landscape as Camus, the personification of the river Cam, and other pastoral figures arrive to mourn. This expansion is structurally deliberate: Milton mimics the digressive, interruptive quality of grief itself, moving from lament to satire to hymn without the linear progression of conventional narrative. The irregular rhyming verse, shifting line lengths and rhyme patterns across 193 lines, creates a flexible music that alternates between lyric intensity, ecclesiastical polemic, and cosmic consolation. Samuel Johnson, in his *Lives of the Poets*, famously criticised this structure as "grossly familiar" pastoral fiction, charging that the poem's "inherent improbability" undermines its sincerity. The debate Johnson initiated, whether pastoral convention obscures or enables genuine mourning, remains central to Milton criticism and to examination questions on the pastoral elegy genre.
## Fame, Phoebus, and the Poet's Laborious Days
The Fame digression, interrupting the elegiac narrative at lines 64–84, meditates on the poet's labour and the uncertain reward of glory:

These lines, among the most quoted in Milton's oeuvre, define fame as both motivation and pathology, the "last infirmity of noble mind," the final weakness that even the virtuous cannot shed. The poet's "laborious days," spent in scorn of delights, may yield no memorial: Lycidas lies dead without the laurel crown that fame promises. Phoebus Apollo intervenes to correct the speaker, declaring that fame is not the true reward but "inward ripeness" and the approval of Jove. The digression thus questions the very poetic ambition that the elegy ostensibly serves: if Edward King died before achieving fame, and if fame itself is an "infirmity," what consolation can poetry offer? The interruption is structurally audacious. Milton inserts a debate about the value of his own vocation into the middle of a poem written to commemorate a friend, as though grief could not proceed without first interrogating the art that grief employs.

> Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise  
> (That last infirmity of noble mind)  
> To scorn delights, and live laborious days;  
> (John Milton, *The Complete Shorter Poems*, ed. John Carey, ll. 64–66)
## St Peter's Blind Mouths and Ecclesiastical Satire
The poem's most politically charged passage is spoken by St Peter, figured as the "Pilot of the Galilean lake," who condemns the hireling clergy responsible for the spiritual neglect of their flocks:

The disease imagery, sheep "swoln with wind," rotting "inwardly," spreading "foul contagion", transforms pastoral convention into satire on clerical corruption. The "blind mouths" of line 119 cannot feed their flocks because they feed themselves, drawing "the rank mist" of empty doctrine rather than nourishing truth. The "grim Wolf" with "privy paw" suggests covert predation, perhaps Laudian persecution or sectarian encroachment, while the "two-handed engine" at the door, whether interpreted as the scissors of fate, ecclesiastical censure, or divine judgment, threatens apocalyptic smiting "once, and smite no more." Critics dispute the engine's precise referent, but the passage's general force is clear: Milton pivots from private loss to public indictment, using the pastoral frame to condemn clergy who fail in their pastoral duty. For candidates studying Caroline literature, this speech connects *Lycidas* to the religious polemics that would intensify into Civil War, even as the poem remains formally an elegy for a drowned Cambridge scholar.

> The hungry Sheep look up, and are not fed,  
> But, swoln with wind and the rank mist they draw,  
> Rot inwardly, and foul contagion spread:  
> Besides what the grim Wolf with privy paw  
> Daily devours apace, and nothing said;  
> —But that two-handed engine at the door  
> Stands ready to smite once, and smite no more.  
> (John Milton, *The Complete Shorter Poems*, ed. John Carey, ll. 125–131)
## Resurrection, Consolation, and Fresh Pastures

After further mourning, mythological allusion (Orpheus, dolphins carrying the drowned body), and the intervention of Triton, the poem turns to Christian consolation. The voice of the uncouth swain gives way to a declarative hymn that transforms grief into resurrection hope:

The solar imagery, Lycidas as day-star sunk beneath the watery floor, then risen to flame in the morning sky, converts pagan pastoral into Christian apotheosis. Lycidas is "not dead" but "sunk low, yet mounted high," living "through the dear might of Him that walk'd the waves." The pastoral machinery is finally subsumed by resurrection theology; the fictive shepherds are told to weep no more because their sorrow has been transcended. The poem's closing frame withdraws the mourning swain from the pastoral scene: "Tomorrow to fresh woods, and pastures new." Elegy converts into vocational renewal, the uncouth swain departs, and the poet who will become the author of *Paradise Lost* turns toward his own laborious days.

*Lycidas* has been the model for later elegiac tradition, Shelley's *Adonais*, Tennyson's *In Memoriam*, Auden's "In Memory of W. B. Yeats", and remains essential for Milton studies and UGC NET English syllabi. T. S. Eliot and F. R. Leavis rehabilitated its structural complexity against Johnson's charge of artificiality, arguing that the poem's self-conscious pastoral critique and digressive form enact the very interruptions of grief they appear to violate. Whether one reads *Lycidas* as sincere commemoration, as a virtuoso display of literary learning, or as both simultaneously, its achievement is undisputed: it perfects the English pastoral elegy by gathering classical lament, Christian consolation, and sharp ecclesiastical satire into a single experimental form that prefigures the range of *Paradise Lost*. In mourning Edward King, Milton mourns the poet's vulnerability to early death, the corruption of the church that should nurture young scholars, and the uncertain reward of fame, yet he concludes with a affirmation of resurrection and renewal that has made *Lycidas* the greatest pastoral elegy in the English language.

> Weep no more, woeful shepherds, weep no more,  
> For Lycidas your sorrow is not dead,  
> Sunk though he be beneath the watery floor,  
> So sinks the day-star in the ocean bed,  
> And yet anon repairs his drooping head,  
> And tricks his beams, and with new spangled ore  
> Flames in the forehead of the morning sky:  
> (John Milton, *The Complete Shorter Poems*, ed. John Carey, ll. 165–171)
Andrew Marvell (1621–1678)
Original title: "To His Coy Mistress"
c. 1650s (published 1681) · Early Modern English · English Metaphysical and Cavalier lyric · Commonwealth / Restoration transition · Carpe diem poem in forty-six lines of iambic tetrameter couplets
## World Enough and Time: The Conditional Fantasy of Endless Courtship

Andrew Marvell's "To His Coy Mistress" opens with one of the most seductive conditionals in English poetry, proposing that if time and space were infinite, the lady's coyness would be both excusable and honourable. Composed during the 1650s, probably while Marvell was tutor in the household of Lord Fairfax at Nun Appleton, Yorkshire, the poem circulated in manuscript among coterie readers before its posthumous appearance in *Miscellaneous Poems* (1681), edited by Mary Marvell. The speaker addresses a silent "Coy Mistress" whose identity remains disputed: tradition links her to Fairfax's daughter Mary, yet the poem's lady is equally plausible as a generic figure of Petrarchan resistance. What is certain is the poem's formal architecture: a three-part logical argument, If, But, Therefore, that imports the rigour of scholastic syllogism into the rhetoric of seduction, a hallmark of Metaphysical method inherited from Donne and sharpened by Marvell's peculiar blend of wit, pastoral expansiveness, and sudden graveyard terror.
The opening section imagines a courtship so leisurely that geography itself must be rearranged to accommodate it:

The hyperbole is simultaneously playful and philosophically pointed. India and Yorkshire, the Ganges and the Humber, map the lovers onto opposite ends of the known world, converting erotic separation into a cosmic geography that no actual courtship could traverse. The temporal scale is equally extravagant: love "ten years before the Flood" and refusal "till the conversion of the Jews" invoke biblical eschatology to measure a courtship longer than sacred history itself. The "vegetable love" conceit, love growing like a plant, "vaster than empires, and more slow", yokes organic patience to imperial magnitude, suggesting that true devotion expands without haste. Yet the very extravagance of the fantasy exposes its impossibility. The conditional "Had we but world enough, and time" quietly announces that we do not. For UGC NET English candidates, this opening exemplifies how Metaphysical poetry conducts argument through scale: the larger the hypothetical world, the more urgently the real world's limits will press upon the poem's second movement.

> Had we but world enough, and time,  
> This coyness, lady, were no crime.  
> We would sit down and think which way  
> To walk, and pass our long love's day;  
> Thou by the Indian Ganges' side  
> Shouldst rubies find: I by the tide  
> Of Humber would complain. I would  
> Love you ten years before the Flood,  
> And you should, if you please, refuse  
> Till the conversion of the Jews.  
> My vegetable love should grow  
> Vaster than empires, and more slow;  
> (Nigel Smith, ed., "To His Coy Mistress", ll. 1–12)
## The Wingèd Chariot and the Marble Vault: Time as Predator

At line 21 the poem executes its famous tonal volta. The adversative "But" shatters the leisurely conditional with a memento mori so grotesque that it transforms carpe diem from Horatian invitation into existential indictment:

Time's "wingèd chariot" personifies temporality as an active pursuer, Phaethon's solar vehicle repurposed as the instrument of mortality's hunt. Behind the lovers lies not pastoral repose but "deserts of vast eternity," a phrase that empties the future of all human content, reducing posthumous existence to an unpeopled wasteland. The shift from marble vault to worm is Marvell's most shocking anti-pastoral gesture: the lady's preserved honour, her "quaint" virtue maintained through coy refusal, will be tested not by a lover but by grave worms that mock the very concept of bodily integrity. Honour "turn to dust" and lust "into ashes" place erotic desire and social virtue on the same terminal trajectory, exposing coyness as a strategy that defers pleasure without defeating death. The closing couplet's grim wit, "The grave's a fine and private place, / But none I think do there embrace", delivers its punch through understatement, as though the speaker were offering travel advice about an inn where no guest ever checks out. Feminist criticism has rightly interrogated the coercive logic of this passage: the lady's silence throughout the poem leaves her no rebuttal to an argument that converts her modesty into futility. Whether Marvell ironises or endorses the speaker's rhetoric remains among the poem's most productive critical disputes.

> But at my back I always hear  
> Time's wingèd chariot hurrying near;  
> And yonder all before us lie  
> Deserts of vast eternity.  
> Thy beauty shall no more be found,  
> Nor, in thy marble vault, shall sound  
> My echoing song; then worms shall try  
> That long preserv'd virginity,  
> And your quaint honour turn to dust,  
> And into ashes all my lust:  
> The grave's a fine and private place,  
> But none I think do there embrace.  
> (Nigel Smith, ed., "To His Coy Mistress", ll. 21–32)
## Birds of Prey and the Iron Gates: Erotic Energy Against Chronology
The imperative "Therefore" section converts terror into urgency, urging consummation while youth and desire remain combustible:

The volta from death-imagery to erotic invitation is among the poem's greatest technical achievements. "Morning dew" on the skin restores pastoral delicacy after the graveyard grotesque, while "instant fires" transpiring "at every pore" suggest that desire is already visible, already legible in the lady's body, a rhetorical move that presumes consent the poem never grants her voice to confirm. The simile of "am'rous birds of prey" inverts conventional carpe diem imagery: where Herrick's virgins gather rosebuds, Marvell's lovers hunt, devouring time rather than being devoured by it. The predatory birds transform the passive victimhood of section two into active aggression, as though erotic consummation were the only adequate response to temporal predation. The editorial dispute over "glew" (1681) versus "dew" (modern emendation) in line 34 carries interpretive weight: "glew" suggests viscous, adhesive youth; "dew" preserves pastoral transience. Either reading reinforces the section's central claim, that beauty and desire are perishable commodities that must be spent before Time's "slow-chapp'd power" grinds them away.

> Now therefore, while the youthful hue  
> Sits on thy skin like morning dew,  
> And while thy willing soul transpires  
> At every pore with instant fires,  
> Now let us sport us while we may,  
> And now, like am'rous birds of prey,  
> Rather at once our time devour  
> Than languish in his slow-chapp'd power.  
> (Nigel Smith, ed., "To His Coy Mistress", ll. 33–40)
## Rolling Strength into One Ball: Joshua's Sun Inverted
The closing movement gathers the poem's energies into a single image of violent synthesis:

The ball conceit, whether cannonball, sphere of compounded force, or alchemical unity, compresses strength and sweetness into a projectile aimed at life's barriers. "Tear our pleasures with rough strife / Thorough the iron gates of life" replaces courtly delicacy with martial assault, as though consummation required breaching fortifications that coyness and mortality jointly maintain. The final couplet inverts the biblical miracle of Joshua 10:12–13, where the sun stood still to extend daylight for battle. Marvell's lovers cannot halt the sun, but they can "make him run"—forcing time to accelerate in sympathy with their passion, converting temporal pressure into erotic triumph. The iambic tetrameter couplets, brisk throughout the poem's forty-six lines, enact this acceleration at the level of metre: the tetrameter line moves faster than pentameter, and the rhyming couplets drive each argumentative section to epigrammatic closure.

> Let us roll all our strength, and all  
> Our sweetness, up into one ball;  
> And tear our pleasures with rough strife  
> Thorough the iron gates of life:  
> Thus, though we cannot make our sun  
> Stand still, yet we will make him run.  
> (Nigel Smith, ed., "To His Coy Mistress", ll. 41–46)
## Marvell the Chameleon: Between Donne, Herrick, and Modernism

"To His Coy Mistress" occupies a unique position in seventeenth-century lyric. It inherits Donne's argumentative structure and startling conceits, yet its pastoral expansiveness and Cavalier grace align it with Herrick and Waller, poets whose carpe diem poems Marvell subverts through graveyard darkness. Nigel Smith's biography titles Marvell "The Chameleon," and this poem justifies the epithet: the same voice that praises vegetable love's imperial slowness can, within twenty lines, imagine worms violating virginity and, within another ten, command birds-of-prey eroticism. The poem's political context, the Commonwealth years, Marvell's service to Fairfax and later to Cromwell, his eventual MPship for Hull, does not surface explicitly, yet the urgency of its temporal argument may resonate with an era in which public time itself seemed catastrophically accelerated by civil war and revolution.

Reception has been continuous and transformative. T. S. Eliot's "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" echoes Marvell's cadences and hesitations, cementing the poem's modernist afterlife. Annabel Patterson's historicist criticism reads Marvell's lyrics within the "writer in public life," reminding us that the tutor-poet who composed this seduction was the same man who would defend religious toleration in prose. For comparative study, the poem belongs in conversation with Horace's *Odes* I.11, Catullus's impatient love poems, Herrick's "To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time," and Donne's "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning"—each testing how long love can afford to wait.

In three movements of mounting intensity, Marvell conducts us from infinite hypothetical courtship through mortal terror to passionate imperative. "To His Coy Mistress" remains the supreme English carpe diem poem because it does more than invite pleasure before beauty fades; it constructs an argument in which pleasure becomes the only rational response to the certainty of bodily annihilation. The coy mistress never speaks, yet her silence structures the poem's drama: she is the audience whose resistance the speaker must overcome, the beauty that time will erase, and the conscience that the poem's wit never quite allows to answer back. Whether one reads the speaker as eloquent lover, coercive rhetorician, or ironic performer, the poem's achievement is undisputed, it fuses logical form, tonal modulation, and metaphysical conceit into a seduction that has outlasted every mistress it ever addressed.

Original title: Haiku (hokku); principal collections include *Oku no Hosomichi* (奥の細道, *The Narrow Road to the Deep North*) and *Sarashina kikō*

c. 1684–1694 (major travel verses 1689; *Oku no Hosomichi* published posthumously 1702) · Classical Japanese (Edo-period literary language) · Japanese haikai; Edo-period *kikō bungaku* (travel literature) · Edo Period; transition from Danrin-school wit to *sabi*, *wabi*, and *karumi* · Haiku (hokku) in 5-7-5 morae; autonomous verses derived from collaborative *renga*
## The Old Pond and the Sound of Water: Hokku as Event

At the centre of world literature's most compressed lyric tradition stands a seventeen-syllable verse composed in 1686 at Bashō's hermitage, a poem that transformed the hokku from a subsidiary opening link in collaborative *renga* chains into an autonomous art form capable of philosophical depth in minimal compass:

Matsuo Bashō is the supreme master of haiku and the most influential Japanese poet in global literary history. Born Matsuo Kinsaku in Ueno, Iga Province, he adopted the pen name Bashō, "banana tree", after the plant that grew beside his hermitage, a symbol of the traveller's impermanent dwelling. His career spans the peaceful but stratified Tokugawa era, when internal travel became possible for poets, pilgrims, and monks, and when urban *haikai* schools in Edo competed to produce witty linked verse. Bashō initially flourished within the Danrin school's taste for wordplay and allusion, yet his mature aesthetics, *sabi* (loneliness, transience), *wabi* (rustic simplicity), and late *karumi* (lightness), reject mere cleverness in favour of immediate perception grounded in Buddhist doctrine of impermanence (*mujō*). The frog-pond verse, celebrated in a frog-themed *renga* contest, marks the turning point: an old pond, a frog's plunge, the sound of water. Nothing more is stated; everything is suggested. For UGC NET English and comparative literature syllabi, this hokku is the paradigmatic case study for *kireji* (cutting words), *kigo* (season words), and *shasei* (sketch from life).

The particle *ya* in "furu ike ya" functions as *kireji*, creating a pause that separates scene-setting from event, stillness from disruption. The old pond exists in unbroken quiet until the frog's jump generates the only action the poem records: not the frog itself but "the sound of water." Bashō directs attention to auditory perception, the ripple's acoustic trace, rather than visual description of the animal or the pond's surface. Steven D. Carter and Makoto Ueda's commentaries emphasise that the verse embodies Bashō's directive to write from direct observation, not bookish convention, the frog was heard rather than merely recalled from literary precedent. Ezra Pound's Imagism, particularly "In a Station of the Metro," owes a direct debt to this principle of instant presentation and irreducible image. The 5-7-5 morae structure creates a rhythmic container whose brevity is not poverty but discipline: each syllable must carry maximum suggestiveness.

> 古池や  
> 蛙飛び込む  
> 水の音  
> *(Romanization: furu ike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto)*  
> *(David Landis Barnhill, trans.: an old pond / a frog jumps in / the sound of water)*  
> (Bashō, hokku of 1686; Barnhill, *Bashō's Haiku*, p. 78)
## Cicada, Rock, and Stillness: *Sabi* at Yamadera

Bashō's *Oku no Hosomichi* (1689)—the account of his journey through the deep north, published posthumously in 1702 from his revised 1694 manuscript, interweaves prose travel narrative with hokku that fuse landscape, history, and spiritual insight. At Risshaku-ji (Yamadera), a mountain temple in Yamagata Prefecture, he composes a verse that paradoxically locates sound within absolute silence:

The *kireji* *ya* again opens the verse onto contemplation: "such stillness" establishes a condition so complete that the cicada's summer cry becomes an intrusion that "penetrates the rocks." The paradox, sound filling silence, voice entering stone, embodies *sabi*, the aesthetic of solitude in which beauty resides in decay, age, and the passage of seasons. The cicada is a *kigo* of summer, embedding the verse in the natural calendar and in centuries of Japanese poetic convention, yet Bashō's treatment is not derivative. The mountain temple setting imports Buddhist stillness: the poet-traveller, deliberately wandering off official highways, seeks not scenic tourism but spiritual refinement. Donald Keene's *Anthology of Japanese Literature* places this verse within the *kikō bungaku* tradition of journeying that Saigyō, the itinerant monk-poet of the twelfth century, established as a model for Bashō's wanderings. The prose context of *Oku no Hosomichi* records the physical labour of climbing the temple's rocky path; the hokku distils that exertion into a single perceptual shock, the moment when insect song and mineral permanence meet.

> 閑さや  
> 岩にしみ入る  
> 蝉の声  
> *(Romanization: shizusa ya / iwa ni shimiiru / semi no koe)*  
> *(Barnhill, trans.: such stillness / the cicada's voice / penetrates the rocks)*  
> (*Oku no Hosomichi*, Yamadera section; Barnhill, *Bashō's Haiku*, p. 112)
## Summer Grasses and Warriors' Dreams: History as Transience
At Hiraizumi, site of the fallen Fujiwara clan's former glory, Bashō confronts the ruins of military power and composes one of the most cited historical haiku in the tradition:

"Summer grasses" (*natsukusa*) functions as *kigo*, locating the verse in the season of fullness and decay simultaneously, the grasses that flourish over abandoned battlefields. The warriors (*tsuwamono-domo*) are absent; only their "dreams" (*yume*) leave traces, and even those traces are reduced to the vegetation that covers them. Bashō's journey to the deep north was partly pilgrimage, partly literary quest: he sought the sites of poets and warriors who preceded him, measuring his own transience against theirs. The Fujiwara clan's twelfth-century splendour at Hiraizumi ended in destruction; the poet stands before summer grass and recognises that political power possesses no more permanence than a seasonal plant. The verse's three-line structure enacts the reduction: subject (grasses), possessive genitive (warriors'), noun of residue (dream's traces). No verb appears; the grammar of ruin is nominal, as though history has already completed its action before the poet arrives. For comparative study, this hokku invites dialogue with Homeric *Iliad* battlefields, Chinese Tang-dynasty frontier poems, and the Japanese *Heike monogatari*'s lament that "the proud do not endure", yet Bashō's compression achieves in seventeen morae what epic and chronicle unfold across volumes.

> 夏草や  
> 兵どもが  
> 夢の跡  
> *(Romanization: natsukusa ya / tsuwamono-domo ga / yume no ato)*  
> *(Donald Keene, trans.: summer grasses— / all that remains / of warriors' dreams)*  
> (*Oku no Hosomichi*, Hiraizumi section; Keene, *Anthology of Japanese Literature*, p. 115)
## The Rough Sea, Sado, and the Milky Way: Cosmic Scale
On the Sea of Japan coast during the 1689 journey, viewing the distant island of Sado where exiles were sent, Bashō composes a verse that yokes earthly punishment to celestial vastness:

The *kireji* *ya* follows "rough sea" (*araumi*), the stormy waters of the Japan Sea coast. Sado Island, *yokotau*, stretching, lying across, was a place of political banishment, where dissenters and defeated figures were sent into geographic erasure. Above or beyond this punitive horizon rises *amanogawa*, the Milky Way, the river of heaven that Japanese literary tradition associates with the Tanabata lovers separated by the celestial river they may cross only once a year. Bashō does not state the allegory; he juxtaposes scales. The exile's island and the galaxy coexist in a single perceptual field, as though the poet's gaze from the rough shore encompassed both punishment and infinity. Tang-dynasty poets Li Bai and Du Fu, whom Bashō studied intensively, inform this compression of landscape and cosmos; Zen-inflected meditation on impermanence supplies the spiritual framework that prevents the image from becoming mere picturesque tourism.

> 荒海や  
> 佐渡によこたふ  
> 天の川  
> *(Romanization: araumi ya / Sado ni yokotau / amanogawa)*  
> *(Barnhill, trans.: the rough sea / stretching toward Sado / the Milky Way)*  
> (*Oku no Hosomichi*, Sado passage; Barnhill, *Bashō's Haiku*, p. 118)
## *Karumi*, Death Verse, and the World Afterlife of Haiku

Bashō's late style, *karumi* (lightness), favours plain diction and everyday subjects over heavy allusion and strained wit. Verses from 1693–1694 greet the mundane world rather than withdrawing from it, as though the poet who had mastered *sabi* and *wabi* discovered that spiritual depth could reside in gentleness rather than austerity. His death poem (*jisei*), composed while ill on his final journey, "falling sick on a journey / my dream goes wandering / on a withered field", converts travel, sickness, and dream into a final image of desolation that completes the aesthetic arc from the frog's splash to the wanderer's last breath.

Reception has been both national and global. Bashō's hokku were inscribed on monuments and traditional sites throughout Japan; the frog-pond verse became the most famous haiku in world literature. English translators debate whether to preserve 5-7-5 syllable count in English or prioritise *kireji* effect and seasonal reference: Barnhill and Keene favour semantic fidelity over formal mimicry, a choice that aligns with Bashō's own insistence on lived perception over formalism for its own sake. The *Shin Nihon Koten Bungaku Taikei* edition (Iwanami Shoten, 1995) provides the standard Japanese text for scholarly citation. Feminist and historicist readings interrogate the masculinist culture of *haikai* schools and the poet's social position as professional master (*bashō* as institution as well as individual), yet the verses themselves largely efface the social self in favour of observed phenomenon.

In a handful of morae, Bashō captures what longer traditions achieve through epic machinery: the sound of water disturbing stillness, cicada song penetrating stone, summer grass covering warriors' dreams, the Milky Way spanning a penal island. *Selected Haiku*—whether read through *Oku no Hosomichi* or as autonomous verses, remains essential for comparative literature, world poetry syllabi, and the study of how minimal form generates maximal suggestion. The old pond is still; the frog jumps; the sound remains. That is the entire event, and it is enough.

## Man's First Disobedience: Invocation, Muse, and the Announced Argument

John Milton's *Paradise Lost* opens with an epic invocation that redirects the classical tradition from pagan triumph to Christian theodicy, announcing a subject "unattempted yet in prose or rhyme" and a purpose that will govern four centuries of interpretation:

Conceived as a drama on the Fall c. 1640–1642, reconceived as epic c. 1657, and substantially complete by 1663–1665, the poem was dictated by a blind Milton to amanuenses including Andrew Marvell and his daughters before its publication by Samuel Simmons in 1667. The opening lines state subject (Adam's disobedience), consequence (death, loss of Eden), and resolution ("one greater Man"—Christ), then invoke a muse that is simultaneously the Holy Spirit of Genesis creation, the inspiration of Moses on Sinai, and the classical Aonian mount surpassed by Milton's "advent'rous song." The announced argument, "to justify the ways of God to men", commits the epic to theodicy: the defence of divine justice in the face of evil and suffering. For UGC NET English candidates, this proem establishes the poem's double inheritance from Homer and Virgil on one hand and Genesis, Revelation, and Dante on the other, while Milton's rejection of rhyme, defended in the 1674 note "The Verse", frees blank verse for syntactic complexity, enjambment, and the epic grandeur that would define serious English narrative poetry for generations.

## Better to Reign in Hell: Satan's Charisma and the Burning Lake

Book I narrates Satan's awakening on the burning lake of Hell, his rallying of Beelzebub, and the speeches that have generated the most enduring controversy in Milton criticism: whether Satan is the poem's true hero. William Blake's claim that Milton was "of the Devil's party without knowing it" inaugurates the Romantic Satanist reading that finds in the fallen archangel a magnificence the theological framework cannot contain:

Satan defines heroism as interior fortitude: the "unconquerable Will," "immortal hate," and refusal to "submit or yield." The rhetoric is Stoic and republican, resonating with Milton's own experience of defeated Commonwealth idealism in the aftermath of Civil War, regicide, and Restoration. To "bow and sue for grace" would be ignominy worse than defeat itself, a sentiment that maps easily onto the poet who served Cromwell's government and lived to see monarchy restored. Yet the poem's structure gradually exposes Satan's self-deception: the charisma of Book I will erode across twelve books as the rebel who claims unconquerability becomes a serpent grovelling in dust.
The mind-as-place conceit delivers Satan's most quoted antithesis:

Stoic interiority here becomes satanic pathology: the mind's freedom to reinterpret Hell as Heaven is also the freedom to lie to oneself. "Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heav'n" compresses Milton's entire debate about obedience, tyranny, and legitimate authority into a single line that political allegorists have read as commentary on Stuart monarchy, Commonwealth republicanism, and the psychology of rebellion itself. Stanley Fish's *Surprised by Sin* argues that the poem seduces readers into admiring Satan before correcting that admiration, a pedagogical structure that "justifies God's ways" by teaching us to recognise sinful sympathy.

## Awake, Arise: Pandemonium and Epic Machinery Inverted
Satan's command to his fallen legions parodies Christ's resurrection language in demonic inversion, converting gospel rhetoric into epic rallying cry:

The single line echoes Matthew 9:5, "Arise, take up thy bed, and walk", and the broader New Testament vocabulary of spiritual awakening, yet here it summons devils to rebuild their kingdom in Hell. Pandemonium, the capital Satan's hosts construct, becomes the poem's great emblem of magnificent futility: epic architecture devoted to a cause that providence has already foreseen and defeated. Book II's council debate, whether to wage open war, practise guerrilla harassment, or corrupt the new creation of Man, gives the epic psychological and political depth uncommon in classical models. Beelzebub's proposal to attack humanity through fraud rather than force establishes the narrative trajectory toward Eden and the Fall.

The poem's scope expands across twelve books (ten in the first edition): Raphael's narration of the war in Heaven and the creation (Books V–VIII); Satan's journey through Chaos and deception of Uriel (Book III); the description of Paradise and Satan's jealous soliloquy at sight of Adam and Eve (Book IV); the temptation, Fall, and mutual guilt of Book IX; the Son's judgment, Sin and Death's bridge to Earth, and the lovers' reconciliation in Book X; Michael's prophetic vision of human history and the expulsion in Books XI–XII. Barbara Lewalski's critical biography emphasises Milton's gathering of classical epic, Christian theology, and personal defeat into a form that establishes blank verse as the standard for serious English narrative. Epic similes, Satan compared to Leviathan, fallen angels to autumn leaves, slow narrative time and magnify scale, while Galileo's telescope, named in Book I, imports contemporary cosmological debate into the poem's universe.

> Awake, arise, or be for ever fall'n.

## Eden, Eve, and the World Before Them: The Fall and Its Aftermath

Book IX, which Milton considered the poem's dramatic climax, narrates the Fall through Satan's serpentine temptation of Eve, her persuasion of Adam, and the immediate transformation of paradise into shame:

The tree of knowledge tests the hierarchy of created beings: obedience, not intellectual deprivation, is the poem's definition of virtue. Feminist criticism has long debated Eve's status, whether Milton's portrait reinforces patriarchal subordination or grants Eve a rationality and agency that complicate simple condemnation. The twelve-book revision of 1674 splits the final movement into Michael's vision of humanity's future (war, flood, incarnation, crucifixion) and the couple's expulsion, a structural change that some critics find diluting and others find theologically clarifying.
The poem closes not on despair but on companionship and providential hope:

Adam and Eve depart Paradise with "the world was all before them"—the Fall irreversible, yet redemptive history already inscribed in the epic's opening promise of "one greater Man." The ending converts epic loss into vocational beginning, prefiguring the Christian narrative the poem has justified through its entire machinery.

> They, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow,  
> Through Eden took their solitary way.  
> (Fowler, ed., *Paradise Lost*, Book XII, ll. 648–649)
## Blake, Johnson, and the Epic That Defined English Poetry

Reception of *Paradise Lost* mirrors its internal tensions. Samuel Johnson praises the poem's sublimity while questioning its theological argument and the credibility of its supernatural machinery. Romantic poets, Wordsworth, Shelley, Keats, engage deeply with Miltonic language and Satanic charisma. T. S. Eliot and F. R. Leavis rehabilitate its structural complexity against charges of excessive learning. The poem becomes foundational for English literature, UGC NET syllabi, and subsequent epic and dystopian fiction from Pullman to Lewis.

Disputed questions sustain its analytical richness: whether Satan is hero or villain; how Milton's republican politics map onto rebellion; whether Eve is subordinate agent or tragic figure; whether the ten-book or twelve-book structure is superior. What remains undisputed is the poem's achievement: it gathers Homer, Virgil, Dante, Spenser, and Genesis into blank verse that "justifies the ways of God to men" while creating the most charismatic rebel in English literature, a figure whose magnificence the poem's theology condemns yet whose rhetoric it cannot forget. In *Paradise Lost*, Milton mourns the Commonwealth, confronts his own blindness, and constructs an epic cosmos in which the Fall is both catastrophe and commencement. The Heavenly Muse invoked on Oreb and Sinai broods still over the vast abyss of critical interpretation, and the burning lake reflects every reader who has ever wondered whether, after all, it might be better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.
