Original title: "The Hollow Men"

Written 1923–1925; first published November 1925 · English (with Conradian epigraph) · High Modernism; post–*Waste Land* spiritual allegory; Anglo-American interwar despair · Five-part allegorical poem (98 lines); fragmented lyric with refrains, nursery-rhyme cadence, and Dantean-Conradian framework
## Mistah Kurtz and Guy Fawkes: Conrad, Dante, and the Land of Hollow Men

T. S. Eliot's "The Hollow Men"—composed 1923–1925 in the aftermath of *The Waste Land* and Eliot's turn toward Anglo-Catholic belief, first published in *Poetry* (November 1925) and collected in the same year's volume, occupies the spiritual threshold between despair and conversion. The double epigraph collates Joseph Conrad's *Heart of Darkness* with English folk ritual:

Kurtz's reported death from the Congo interior and the Guy Fawkes effigy, penny for the hollow straw man burned on Bonfire Night, juxtapose colonial horror with nursery-rhyme violence, announcing the poem's method of collaging sacred and trivial registers. Dante's *Inferno*, Canto III, where the neutrals who lived without infamy or praise inhabit the ante-Hell of mist and broken stone, informs the poem's "death's dream kingdom" without serving as printed epigraph. Guy Fawkes's hollow straw effigy anticipates the hollow men themselves: stuffed, headpiece filled with straw, leaning together in a field. Grover Smith's *T. S. Eliot's Poetry and Plays* and David Moody's biography situate the poem between *The Waste Land*'s fragmentation and *Ash-Wednesday*'s prayer; for UGC NET English candidates tracing Eliot's religious development, "The Hollow Men" marks the nadir of spiritual emptiness before the turn toward orthodoxy.
Part I introduces the speakers as collective nightmare:

Hollowness and stuffing paradoxically coexist: the men are simultaneously empty and artificially filled. Dried voices, dry grass, dry cellar, parched repetition enacts spiritual aridity without water's redemptive possibility (so central to *The Waste Land*). Rat imagery and broken glass suggest post-war urban ruin and verminous survival rather than heroic suffering.

> Mistah Kurtz—he dead  
> A penny for the Old Guy  
> (Eliot, "The Hollow Men", epigraph; 1925 text)

> We are the hollow men  
> We are the stuffed men  
> Leaning together  
> Headpiece filled with straw. Alas!  
> Our dried voices, when  
> We whisper together  
> Are quiet and meaningless  
> As wind in dry grass  
> Or rats' feet over broken glass  
> In our dry cellar  
> (Eliot, "The Hollow Men", Part I, ll. 1–11; 1925 text)
## Shape Without Form: Conrad's Kurtz and the Colonised Soul
Part II relocates the hollow men to a "dead land" and "cactus land" where shape, shade, and gesture lack substance:

"Death's dream kingdom" sustains Dantean atmosphere while refusing the clarity of damnation or salvation. Eyes, recalling Conrad's Kurtz in *Heart of Darkness*, whom Marlow cannot face and whose last words ("The horror!") Eliot had contemplated as epigraph for *The Waste Land*, haunt without appearing. Sunlight on broken column images classical ruin within tropical desolation; the tree swinging and distant voices offer beauty without access.
Part III's refrain crystallises the poem's diagnosis of modern spiritual condition:

Prayers to broken stone replace living worship; lips that would kiss form only futile supplication. The fading star, perhaps the Star of Bethlehem dimmed, signals exhausted revelation. Eliot's hollow men inhabit the space between life and death, unable to complete either eros or devotion.

> Eyes I dare not meet in dreams  
> In death's dream kingdom  
> These do not appear:  
> There, the eyes are  
> Sunlight on a broken column  
> There, is a tree swinging  
> And voices are  
> In the wind's singing  
> More distant and more solemn  
> Than a fading star.  
> (Eliot, "The Hollow Men", Part II, ll. 19–28; 1925 text)

> This is the dead land  
> This is cactus land  
> Here the stone images  
> Are raised, here they receive  
> The supplication of a dead man's hand  
> Under the twinkle of a fading star.  
> Is it like this  
> In death's other kingdom  
> Waking alone  
> At the hour when we are  
> Trembling with tenderness  
> Lips that would kiss  
> Form prayers to broken stone.  
> (Eliot, "The Hollow Men", Part III, ll. 29–42; 1925 text)
## Multifoliate Rose and Prickly Pear: Prayer Fragmented and the Nursery-Rhyme Abyss
Part IV introduces the multifoliate rose, Dante's celestial symbol in the *Paradiso*, corrupted into prickly pear cactus:

The beach of the tumid river recalls Dante's Acheron and Styx, souls awaiting passage, yet here grope together avoiding speech. Multifoliate rose of Dante's heavenly vision becomes hope only of empty men, inverted within twilight rather than dawn. Part V constitutes the poem's most experimental collapse of language into incantatory failure.

> The eyes are not here  
> There are no eyes here  
> In this valley of dying stars  
> In this hollow valley  
> This broken jaw of our lost kingdoms  
> In this last of meeting places  
> We grope together  
> And avoid speech  
> Gathered on this beach of the tumid river  
> Sightless, unless  
> The eyes reappear  
> As the perpetual star  
> Multifoliate rose  
> Of death's twilight kingdom  
> The hope only  
> Of empty men.  
> (Eliot, "The Hollow Men", Part IV, ll. 43–58; 1925 text)
## Not with a Bang but a Whimper: Lord's Prayer, Nursery Rhyme, and History's Dim End
Part V intercuts the Lord's Prayer with children's song, producing sacred parody:

"Here we go round the mulberry bush" becomes prickly pear, a desert plant replacing cultivated growth. "Between the idea / And the reality / Falls the Shadow" diagnoses modern paralysis: thought cannot reach act, desire cannot reach spasm, essence cannot descend into existence. The Shadow falls between every pairing, and into the Lord's Prayer itself, "For thine is the Kingdom", which fragments across stanzas until only "For Thine is the / Life is / For Thine is the" remains, syntax broken like hollow men.

The closing lines invert popular expectation of apocalyptic bang (perhaps alluding to H. G. Wells or cosmic catastrophe) with whimper, history, personal and civilisational, expiring without climax. Eliot's note that Guy Fawkes epigraph and Conrad's Kurtz inform the hollow stuffed men links political violence, colonial horror, and spiritual vacuity. Five parts progress from collective introduction through dream kingdoms to prickly-pear round-dance and prayer collapse.

Critics debate whether the poem anticipates Eliot's conversion or records permanent condition; the multifoliate rose's brief appearance suggests hope the poem's form cannot sustain. Compared to *The Waste Land*'s multilingual collage, "The Hollow Men" restricts diction to simple repetition and nursery cadence, emptiness made formal through diminishment rather than abundance.

In five parts and ninety-eight lines, Eliot conducts us from hollow stuffed men and dried voices through death's dream kingdom, prayers to broken stone, valley of dying stars, and fragmented Lord's Prayer to the world's whimpering end. "The Hollow Men" remains the definitive expression of interwar spiritual vacuity: the claim that between idea and reality falls the Shadow, that lips form prayers to stone rather than kisses, and that civilisation may expire not with bang but whimper. The poem does more than describe post-war emptiness; by collapsing sacred prayer into nursery rhyme and truncating "For thine is the Kingdom" mid-phrase, it enacts the hollowness it names, a formal stuffing of straw where substance should reside, and the most whispered anticlimax modernist elegy inherits as its prayer's broken conclusion.

Ezra Pound (1885–1972)
Original title: *The Cantos* (Canto XLV: "With Usura")

*The Cantos* composed 1915–1969; Canto XLV first published 1937 (*Fifth Decad of Cantos*) · English (with Italian, Latin, and French fragments) · High Modernism; Anglo-American experimental epic; Imagist and Vorticist poetics · Fragment of a long modernist epic in free verse; liturgical-anaphoric condemnation; one canto within a projected "poem containing history"
## With Usura: Litany, Usury, and the Fifth Decad

Ezra Pound's *The Cantos*—begun c. 1915 and published in instalments through the poet's lifetime, with the complete text appearing posthumously in 1970, constitutes the most ambitious and controversial historical epic in twentieth-century Anglophone poetry. Pound conceives the work as a "poem containing history," assembling fragments of myth, economics, politics, art history, and personal testimony without explanatory transitions. Canto XLV, first published in the *Fifth Decad of Cantos* (1937), stands among the most formally concentrated and politically explicit sections: a rhythmic litany against *usura* (usury), the lending of money at interest, which Pound treats as a civilisational poison corrupting craft, art, fertility, and sacred ritual. Hugh Kenner's *The Pound Era* and Carroll F. Terrell's *A Companion to The Cantos of Ezra Pound* anchor examination scholarship. For UGC NET English candidates tracing modernism's economic and formal experiments, Canto XLV exemplifies Pound's ideogrammic method, juxtaposing concrete particulars without connective syntax to force us to infer relation, and his deployment of medieval English diction to indict contemporary finance.
The canto opens by repeating its central noun as incantation:

Anaphoric "with usura" structures the passage like a responsorial psalm or legal indictment. Medieval verb forms, *hath*, *receiveth*, distance the diction from contemporary prose and lend the condemnation liturgical gravity. Good stone houses require blocks cut smooth and well fitting so that design may cover their face; painted church paradises require harp and light (*harpes et luz*) where the Virgin receives her annunciation and halo projects from incision. Usury, by Pound's logic, prevents both: it substitutes haste and profit for the slow collaboration between material, craftsman, and sacred purpose.

> With usura  
> hath no man a house of good stone  
> each block cut smooth and well fitting  
> that design might cover their face,  
> hath no man a painted paradise on his church wall  
> harpes et luz  
> or where virgin receiveth message  
> and halo projects from incision,  
> (Pound, *The Cantos*, Canto XLV, ll. 1–8; *Fifth Decad of Cantos*, 1937)
## Rusteth the Chisel: Corruption of Art, Craft, and Market
The canto's middle movement names usura's damage to makers and materials in lines that critics have anthologised as Pound's most quotable economic protest:

Repetition enacts corrosion: the chisel rusts, the craft rusts, the craftsman rusts, the sentence in the book is gnawed. Stone cutter and weaver are kept from their materials; wool fails to reach market; sheep bring no gain. The epithet "whoreson usura" intensifies moral revulsion while preserving the canto's pseudo-medieval register. Earlier lines establish that under usura no Gonzaga may see his heirs and concubines in enduring art, no picture is made to live with but to "sell and sell quickly." Pound links Renaissance patronage to pre-capitalist exchange where art serves dynasty and devotion rather than speculative return. The formal strategy is not argument in the essayistic sense but accretion: each repeated phrase adds another domain, architecture, fresco, sculpture, weaving, husbandry, to the catalogue of ruin.

> usura rusteth the chisel  
> It rusteth the craft and the craftsman  
> It gnaweth the sentence in the book  
> It hath a triple canker  
> usura rusteth the chisel  
> It rusteth the craft and the craftsman  
> It gnaweth the sentence in the book  
> with usura  
> stone cutter is kept from his stone  
> weaver is kept from his loom  
> Wool comes not to market  
> Sheep bringeth no gain with usura  
> whoreson usura  
> (Pound, *The Cantos*, Canto XLV, ll. 15–26; *Fifth Decad of Cantos*, 1937)
## Pietro Lombardo Came Not: Masters, Syntax, and Ideogrammic Juxtaposition
Canto XLV's counter-litany invokes artists and monuments created without usurious finance:

Pound names Venetian and Tuscan masters, Pietro Lombardo, Duccio, Piero della Francesca, Giovanni Bellini, Fra Angelico, Ambrogio Preda, alongside Botticelli's *La Calunnia* and Romanesque churches at Saint-Trophime and Saint-Hilaire whose stones bear the mason's signature *Adamo me fecit*. The ideogrammic method operates here through parataxis: no causal conjunction explains how patronage without usury produced these works; us must infer that interest-bearing credit severs the bond between maker, material, and enduring form. Dante places usurers in the seventh circle of *Inferno*, hands bound and exposed to falling flames, a precedent Pound's economic cantos repeatedly invoke. Canto XLV's compressed syntax, dropped articles, and Middle English verb endings create what Terrell calls a "language of indictment" distinct from the documentary collage elsewhere in *The Cantos*.

> with usura  
> Pietro Lombardo came not by usura  
> Duccio came not by usura  
> nor Pier della Francesca; Zuan Bellin' not by usura  
> nor was "La Calunnia" painted.  
> Came not by usura Angelico; came not Ambrogio Praedis,  
> Came no church of cut stone signed: Adamo me fecit.  
> Not by usura St. Trophime  
> Not by usura Saint Hilaire,  
> (Pound, *The Cantos*, Canto XLV, ll. 39–47; *Fifth Decad of Cantos*, 1937)
## Contra Naturam: Fertility, Ritual, and Epic Fragment
The canto's climax broadens usura from aesthetic corruption to assault on biological and sacramental order:

Usury slays the child in the womb, stays courtship, brings palsy between bride and bridegroom. The Latin heading *CONTRA NATURAM* (against nature) frames the charge in scholastic and canon-law vocabulary Pound absorbed through economic historians such as A. R. Orage and later through his own broadcasts. The Eleusinian mysteries, ancient rites of grain and renewal, are profaned: whores substitute for priestesses, corpses banquet at the wedding feast. The image fuses sexual sterility, monetary abstraction, and sacrilege into a single ideogram. Closing lines return to stale bread made of rags, repeating with increasing compression until language itself seems gnawed by the triple canker named earlier.

Immediately controversial for its antisemitic contexts within Pound's broader economic writings and wartime propaganda, Canto XLV nevertheless remains central to modernist debates about poetry and political economy. Its litany structure influenced protest verse and performance poetry; its craft-centred ethics resonate with William Morris's socialism and with contemporary critiques of financialisation. Within *The Cantos* as a whole, XLV provides a formal pause, a single-note anaphoric chant amid the polyglot documentary chaos of adjacent cantos, demonstrating that Pound's epic attains rhetorical clarity when it abandons annotation for incantation.

In one canto of liturgical repetition and medieval syntax, Pound conducts us from stone houses and church-wall paradises through rusted chisels and thwarted weavers to Renaissance masters who came not by usura, and from slain children and palsied bridegrooms to whores at Eleusis and corpses at the wedding feast. Canto XLV remains the definitive expression of High Modernist economic indictment within epic form: the claim that usura rusteth craft and craftsman, that art made to sell quickly cannot endure, and that corruption of exchange is corruption of nature itself. The canto does more than describe that thesis; by repeating "with usura" until syntax fractures and masters are named in paratactic procession, it enacts the litany method and ideogrammic juxtaposition that *The Cantos* inherits as its most concentrated fusion of medieval diction and modernist fragmentation.

> Slayeth the child in the womb  
> It stayeth the young man's courting  
> It hath brought palsy to bed, lyeth  
> between the young bride and her bridegroom  
> CONTRA NATURAM  
> They have brought whores for Eleusis  
> Corpses are set to banquet  
> at the wedding feast  
> (Pound, *The Cantos*, Canto XLV, ll. 27–33; *Fifth Decad of Cantos*, 1937)
Rainer Maria Rilke (1875–1926)
Original title: *Duineser Elegien* (Erste Elegie)

Composed 1912–1922; first published 1923 (*Insel-Verlag*, Leipzig) · German · German-language Modernism; late Symbolist and existential lyric; Austro-Hungarian and Weimar-era poetry · First of ten elegies in irregular free verse (858 lines in the complete cycle); meditative apostrophe addressing angels, the dead, and the limits of human praise
## Who If I Cried Out: Duino, Angels, and the Opening Question

Rainer Maria Rilke's *Duino Elegies*—begun at Duino Castle on the Adriatic in January 1912, interrupted by the First World War and personal crisis, and completed in a February 1922 burst at Château de Muzot in the Rhône Valley, constitute the summit of German-language lyric modernism. Rilke described the opening of the First Elegy as arriving "as if dictated" during a winter walk above the sea; the completed cycle was first published by Insel-Verlag, Leipzig, in 1923. The ten elegies address human transience, the task of transforming visible reality into inwardness, and the terrifying proximity of angels as emblems of absolute beauty. Stephen Mitchell's English translation (1982) and J. B. Leishman and Stephen Spender's earlier version (1939) anchor Anglophone study; Kathleen M. Woodham's commentary and Heidegger's lectures on Rilke contextualise the philosophical reception. For UGC NET English candidates tracing European modernism's spiritual vocabulary, the First Elegy establishes the cycle's governing paradox: the angel is not a consoling messenger but a symbol of beauty so intense that proximity would annihilate the human speaker.
The elegy opens with a question that defines the human position between silence and transcendence:

Crying out among the angelic hierarchies would receive no answer, or worse, an answer that consumes. Beauty is nothing but the beginning of terror we are still just able to endure; the angel's serenity lies in disdaining annihilation while remaining terrifying. The speaker therefore holds himself back and swallows the call-note of dark sobbing. Apostrophe replaces dialogue: whom can we turn to in need? Not angels, not humans.

> Who, if I cried out, would hear me among the angels' hierarchies?  
> and even if one of them pressed me suddenly against his heart:  
> I would be consumed in that overwhelming existence.  
> For beauty is nothing but the beginning of terror,  
> which we are still just able to endure,  
> and we are so awed because it serenely disdains  
> to annihilate us. Every angel is terrifying.  
> (Rilke, *Duino Elegies*, First Elegy, ll. 1–7; trans. Stephen Mitchell, 1982; German text *Duineser Elegien*, 1923)
## Weltinnenraum: The Interpreted World and Inward Transformation

The First Elegy develops Rilke's concept of *Weltinnenraum*—world-inner-space, the process by which outer phenomena are absorbed into consciousness until landscape becomes psyche. The knowing animals already sense human estrangement:

We are not at home in our interpreted world, the world human consciousness has translated into symbol and concept. What remains are modest anchors: a tree taken daily into vision, yesterday's street, the loyalty of habit that moved in and never left. Night brings a wind full of infinite space that gnaws at faces; lovers use each other to hide their own fate. Rilke instructs us to fling the emptiness out of arms into the spaces we breathe, so that birds may feel expanded air with more passionate flying. *Weltinnenraum* names the elegy's constructive task: not to escape the physical world but to internalise it so completely that vision and object merge, a theory Rilke articulates in his 1914 essay on dolls and in letters to Witold Hulewicz, and that distinguishes his modernism from Symbolist withdrawal.

> and already the knowing animals are aware  
> that we are not really at home in  
> our interpreted world. Perhaps there remains for us  
> some tree on a hillside, which every day we can take  
> into our vision; there remains for us yesterday's street  
> and the loyalty of a habit so much at ease  
> when it stayed with us that it moved in and never left.  
> (Rilke, *Duino Elegies*, First Elegy, ll. 13–20; trans. Stephen Mitchell, 1982; German text *Duineser Elegien*, 1923)
## Springtimes Needed You: Praise, Lovers, and the Bowstring Tension

The elegy's middle movement addresses failed receptivity and the discipline required for genuine praise. Springtimes needed the addressee; stars waited to be noticed; waves rolled from the distant past; violins yielded themselves through open windows, all mission, yet expectation distracted:

Rilke counsels singing of women in love and women abandoned, passions not yet immortal, rather than pursuing a single beloved who cannot be housed among huge strange thoughts. The famous injunction to begin again and again the never-attainable praising links the elegy to Rilke's *Sonnets to Orpheus*, composed in the same February 1922 creative flood:

Gaspara Stampa's fierce objectless love offers a model for deserted girls; suffering must grow fruitful. The elegy's most cited metaphor demands endurance of separation: as the arrow endures the bowstring's tension, gathered in the snap of release to be more than itself, for there is no place where we can remain.

> Yes—the springtimes needed you. Often a star  
> was waiting for you to notice it. A wave rolled toward you  
> out of the distant past, or as you walked  
> under an open window, a violin  
> yielded itself to your hearing. All this was mission.  
> But could you accomplish it? Weren't you always  
> distracted by expectation, as if every event  
> announced a beloved?  
> (Rilke, *Duino Elegies*, First Elegy, ll. 29–36; trans. Stephen Mitchell, 1982; German text *Duineser Elegien*, 1923)

> Begin again and again the never-attainable praising;  
> remember: the hero lives on; even his downfall was  
> merely a pretext for achieving his final birth.  
> But Nature, spent and exhausted, takes lovers back  
> into herself, as if there were not enough strength  
> to create them a second time.  
> (Rilke, *Duino Elegies*, First Elegy, ll. 44–49; trans. Stephen Mitchell, 1982; German text *Duineser Elegien*, 1923)
## Voices and the Dead: Saints, Churches, and German Modernist Inheritance
The closing movement summons voices from silence and addresses the dead who died young:

Saints listened until gigantic call lifted them off the ground while they kept kneeling; the speaker cannot endure God's voice but must listen to wind and the ceaseless message forming from silence. The dead who died young murmur from churches in Naples and Rome, from plaques and eulogies; they ask that injustice about their death be gently removed so souls may proceed onward. Being dead is hard work, full of retrieval before eternity's trace is felt; angels (they say) do not know whether they move among living or dead. The Linus legend, daring first notes of song piercing barren numbness, promises that grief becomes the source of spirit's growth.

Influential across European and Anglophone poetry, the *Duino Elegies* shaped Paul Celan, W. H. Auden, and countless post-war elegists. The First Elegy in particular codifies modernism's angelic anxiety: beauty as terror's threshold, praise as perpetual beginning, and consciousness as an interpreted world we never quite inhabit. Ten elegies in irregular blank verse move from this opening question toward the Ninth Elegy's praise of earthly transience and the Tenth's acceptance of mortality; the First remains the gateway.

In the opening elegy of irregular free verse, Rilke conducts us from the unanswered cry among angelic hierarchies and beauty as beginning of terror through the interpreted world and springtimes' missions to never-attainable praising, Gaspara Stampa's example, and the arrow's bowstring tension, and from voices listened as saints listened to the dead who died young and the Linus legend's piercing song. The First Elegy remains the definitive expression of German modernist spiritual crisis: the claim that every angel is terrifying, that we are not at home in our interpreted world, and that *Weltinnenraum* demands we begin again and again the praising we cannot complete. The elegy does more than state that paradox; by sustaining apostrophe across animals, lovers, heroes, and the dead without narrative resolution, it enacts the tension between human limitation and the overwhelming existence that would consume any cry fully heard.
**Word count (body):** 1,330

> Voices. Voices. Listen, my heart, as only  
> saints have listened: until the gigantic call lifted them  
> off the ground; yet they kept on, impossibly,  
> kneeling and didn't notice at all:  
> so complete was their listening.  
> (Rilke, *Duino Elegies*, First Elegy, ll. 61–65; trans. Stephen Mitchell, 1982; German text *Duineser Elegien*, 1923)
Federico García Lorca (1898–1936)
Original title: "Romance Sonámbulo" (in *Romancero Gitano*)

Composed 1924–1927; first published 1928 (*Revista de Occidente*, Madrid) · Spanish · Generation of '27; Andalusian lyric; Spanish modernism fused with folk ballad · *Romance* (ballad) in octosyllabic verse with assonantal rhyme on even lines; surrealist dream narrative with refrain
## Verde Que Te Quiero Verde: Refrain, Desire, and Romancero Gitano

Federico García Lorca's "Romance Sonámbulo"—composed 1924–1927 and published in *Romancero Gitano* (1928) alongside eighteen other poems that reimagine Andalusian gitano life through modernist myth, is the most anthologised work in modern Spanish poetry. Lorca completed the collection before his 1929–1930 sojourn in New York and dedicated individual poems to friends including Gloria Giner and Fernando de los Ríos. The title compounds *romance* (the traditional Spanish ballad form) with *sonámbulo* (sleepwalker), signalling a narrative that moves by dream logic rather than realistic causation. Ian Gibson's biography and Christopher Maurer, ed., *Collected Poems* (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1991) anchor scholarship; English translations by A. S. Kline and Sarah Arvio circulate widely. For UGC NET English candidates studying European modernism's dialogue with folk forms, "Romance Sonámbulo" exemplifies how the Generation of '27 recovered popular tradition while injecting Surrealist image-combination and symbolist colour symbolism.
The poem's refrain anchors every major section:

Green I want you green: the refrain fuses colour with desire (*verde que te quiero verde* puns on *verde* as colour and as the verb "to appear" or youthful freshness). Green wind, green branches, boat on the sea, horse on the mountain establish the Andalusian landscape in emblem rather than topographical detail. She dreams on her balcony, green flesh, green hair, eyes of cold silver, while the gitano moon renders objects sentient: things watch her and she cannot watch them. Sleepwalking begins here: perception inverts, agency disperses into the natural and lunar world.

> VERDE que te quiero verde.  
> Verde viento. Verdes ramas.  
> El barco sobre la mar  
> y el caballo en la montaña.  
> Con la sombra en la cintura,  
> ella sueña en su baranda,  
> verde carne, pelo verde,  
> con los ojos de fría plata.  
> Verde que te quiero verde.  
> Bajo la luna gitana,  
> las cosas la están mirando  
> y ella no puede mirarlas.  
> (Lorca, "Romance Sonámbulo", ll. 1–14; *Romancero Gitano*, 1928)
## Octosyllabic Assonance: Romance Form and Surrealist Dream Logic

"Romance Sonámbulo" obeys the traditional *romance* structure: octosyllabic lines (eight syllables per line), assonantal rhyme on even lines (here predominantly *-ando* / *-ana* / *-aza* vowel echoes), and tripartite division marked by asterisks. Lorca adapts a form associated with medieval and oral narrative, frontier ballads, Morisco romances, without archaising diction; instead he compresses violent action, erotic longing, and death into images that refuse logical sequencing. The second section intensifies lunar and arboreal hallucination:

Frost stars arrive with the shadow-fish opening dawn's path; the fig tree rubs its wind with branch-rough sandpaper; the mountain as wildcat bristles bitter agaves. Questions, who will come? by what route?, receive no rational answer. She remains on the balcony dreaming of the bitter sea. Surrealist technique, learned from contact with Dalí and Buñuel in the late 1920s, operates through metaphor stacked upon metaphor without explanatory connective: each image is legible locally but resists paraphrase as unified plot.

> Verde que te quiero verde.  
> Grandes estrellas de escarcha  
> vienen con el pez de sombra  
> que abre el camino del alba.  
> La higuera frota su viento  
> con la lija de sus ramas,  
> y el monte, gato garduño,  
> eriza sus pitas agrias.  
> Pero ¿quién vendrá? ¿Y por dónde?...  
> Ella sigue en su baranda,  
> verde carne, pelo verde,  
> soñando en la mar amarga.  
> (Lorca, "Romance Sonámbulo", ll. 15–28; *Romancero Gitano*, 1928)
## Compadre Yo Ya No Soy Yo: Wounded Gypsy, Identity, and Death
The poem's dramatic centre introduces the wounded *compadre* (ritual kinsman) who seeks exchange and sanctuary:

The wounded man offers horse for house, saddle for mirror, knife for blanket; he bleeds from Cabra's ports and asks to die decently in bed, of steel if possible, with Holland sheets. The reply denies stable identity: "I am no longer I, nor is my house my house anymore." Lorca encodes the Spanish ballad's fatal wound motif, lover or rival bleeding across the landscape, within a transaction that cannot close because self and dwelling have already dissolved. Three hundred dark roses stain the white shirt; blood seeps and smells around the sash. The speaker begs to climb to the high railings, the green railings of the moon where water resounds; the compadres ascend leaving trails of blood and tears, tin lanterns trembling on roofs, a thousand crystal tambourines wounding dawn.

> —Compadre, quiero cambiar  
> mi caballo por su casa,  
> mi montura por su espejo,  
> mi cuchillo por su manta.  
> Compadre, vengo sangrando,  
> desde los puertos de Cabra.  
> —Si yo pudiera, mocito,  
> este trato se cerraba.  
> Pero yo ya no soy yo,  
> ni mi casa es ya mi casa.  
> —Compadre, quiero morir  
> decentemente en mi cama.  
> De acero, si puede ser,  
> con las sábanas de holanda.  
> ¿No ves la herida que tengo  
> desde el pecho a la garganta?  
> (Lorca, "Romance Sonámbulo", ll. 29–44; *Romancero Gitano*, 1928)
## Green as Desire and Death: Aljibe, Civil Guard, and Closing Return
The final movement locates the desired woman above the cistern (*aljibe*), sustained by a moon-icicle over water:

The gitana sways over the cistern's face, green flesh, green hair, cold silver eyes, held by an icicle of moon above water. Night becomes intimate as a small plaza; drunk Civil Guards hammer at the door. Authority arrives too late or irrelevantly: the dream-narrative has already completed its ascent to the green balcony. The refrain's return seals the poem as circular sleepwalk: boat and horse remain on sea and mountain; the woman remains desired and unreachable; green marks both erotic vitality and the pallor of death. Critics including José Luis Cano and Andrés Soria Olmedo read *verde* as Lorca's signature colour of desire forbidden by social order, gitano passion observed but never possessed by the speaking compadre who finds only absence ("¿dónde está tu niña amarga?", where is your bitter girl?).

Published months before Lorca's international fame and performed widely before his murder by Nationalist forces in August 1936, *Romancero Gitano* transformed Spanish poetry by proving that folk form could absorb avant-garde image-making without losing musicality. "Romance Sonámbulo" influenced Neruda, Alberti, and subsequent Andalusian verse; its refrain entered popular culture as shorthand for Lorca's lyric universe.

In octosyllabic assonantal verse divided by asterisks, Lorca conducts us from the green refrain and balcony dreamer through frost stars and shadow-fish to the wounded compadre's impossible bargain, the ascent to green railings of the moon, and the gitana swaying over the cistern while Civil Guards hammer at the door. "Romance Sonámbulo" remains the definitive expression of Spanish modernist ballad art: the claim that green names both desire and death, that identity dissolves in sleepwalking narrative ("yo ya no soy yo"), and that the *romance* form can carry Surrealist vision without abandoning oral cadence. The poem does more than describe that night journey; by returning "Verde que te quiero verde" until boat, horse, balcony, and cistern merge in a single chromatic obsession, it enacts the dream logic and assonantal music that *Romancero Gitano* inherits as its most enduring fusion of gitano myth and avant-garde image.

> Sobre el rostro del aljibe  
> se mecía la gitana.  
> Verde carne, pelo verde,  
> con ojos de fría plata.  
> Un carámbano de luna  
> la sostiene sobre el agua.  
> La noche se puso íntima  
> como una pequeña plaza.  
> Guardias civiles borrachos  
> en la puerta golpeaban.  
> Verde que te quiero verde.  
> Verde viento. Verdes ramas.  
> El barco sobre la mar.  
> Y el caballo en la montaña.  
> (Lorca, "Romance Sonámbulo", ll. 73–86; *Romancero Gitano*, 1928)

chapters.title: 78. W. H. Auden: "In Memory of W. B. Yeats"

content.value: Original title: "In Memory of W. B. Yeats"

Written January 1939; first published February 1940 · English · Anglo-American Modernism; interwar elegy; post-Yeatsian meditative lyric · Elegy in three parts with shifting metres and registers (colloquial free verse, reflective meditation, trochaic hymn); occasioned by W. B. Yeats's death (28 January 1939)
## January 1939: A Cold Day and the Death of a Poet

W. H. Auden's "In Memory of W. B. Yeats"—composed in January 1939, within days of W. B. Yeats's death at the Hôtel Idéal Séjour in Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, and first published in *The New Republic* (February 1940) before inclusion in *Another Time* (Random House, 1940)—transforms public mourning into a three-part meditation on poetry's limits and persistence. Auden, who had met Yeats in the 1930s and whose early work owed debts to the Irish poet's Symbolist diction and occult scaffolding, writes from New York as Europe slides toward war. The elegy refuses conventional panegyric: Part I adopts journalistic coldness, Part II delivers a notorious philosophical disclaimer, and Part III ascends into hymnic trochaic tetrameter that charges the dead poet with vocational labour. Edward Mendelson's *Later Auden* and John Fuller's *W. H. Auden: A Commentary* anchor critical readings. For UGC NET English candidates tracing modern elegy from Milton and Shelley to contemporary practice, the poem exemplifies how mid-century poets revise the genre by questioning whether art can redeem political catastrophe.
The opening movement registers death through impersonal geography and weather:

Frozen brooks, deserted airports, and snow disfiguring public statues convert private grief into civilisational atmosphere. Instruments agreeing on a dark cold day suggest meteorological consensus without human consolation, death measured by thermometers and barometers rather than lamentation. Auden's diction here is deliberately flat, almost reportorial, distancing the speaker from Yeatsian lyric warmth. The section's irregular free verse and conversational syntax announce a modern elegy that will not immediately invoke muses or nightingales. Wolves running through evergreen forests and the peasant river untempted by fashionable quays extend the theme: nature and commerce proceed while mourning tongues cannot penetrate the poems themselves.

> He disappeared in the dead of winter:  
> The brooks were frozen, the airports almost deserted,  
> And snow disfigured the public statues;  
> The mercury sank in the mouth of the dying day.  
> What instruments we have agree  
> The day of his death was a dark cold day.  
> (Auden, "In Memory of W. B. Yeats", Part I, ll. 1–6; *Another Time*, 1940)
## Provinces of the Body: Scattered Cities and the Guts of the Living
Part I narrows from continental cold to intimate posthumous dissolution. Yeats's last afternoon becomes a theatre of bodily revolt:

The provinces of the body and squares of the mind map private catastrophe onto civic geography; silence invading suburbs registers psychic evacuation before the poet becomes his admirers, identity dispersed into reception rather than self-possession. Scattered among a hundred cities, Yeats is "wholly given over to unfamiliar affections," punished under foreign codes of conscience. Auden then delivers the elegy's most influential claim about literary afterlife:

Posthumous meaning is digestive, not monumental: readers metabolise the dead poet's language, altering it through interpretation, appropriation, and error. The brokers roaring like beasts on the floor of the bourse, the poor enduring accustomed sufferings, and each person almost convinced of freedom in the cell of himself, Auden juxtaposes Yeats's death with the ordinary violence of markets and solitude. A few thousand will remember the day as slightly unusual; instruments again agree on dark coldness. Part I's colloquial register thus withholds transcendence while insisting on poetry's material circulation through living bodies.

> But for him it was his last afternoon as himself,  
> An afternoon of nurses and rumours;  
> The provinces of his body revolted,  
> The squares of his mind were empty,  
> Silence invaded the suburbs,  
> The current of his feeling failed; he became his admirers.  
> (Auden, "In Memory of W. B. Yeats", Part I, ll. 11–16; *Another Time*, 1940)

> The words of a dead man  
> Are modified in the guts of the living.  
> (Auden, "In Memory of W. B. Yeats", Part I, ll. 22–23; *Another Time*, 1940)
## Poetry Makes Nothing Happen: Mad Ireland and the Valley of Making
Part II shifts metre and tone toward meditative assessment of Yeats's career and poetry's political efficacy:

"Mad Ireland hurt you into poetry" condenses Yeats's nationalist and myth-making career into a single causal phrase, yet Auden immediately qualifies the gift's political efficacy. "Poetry makes nothing happen"—perhaps the most quoted line in twentieth-century poetics, does not deny poetry's value but relocates it: art survives in the valley of its making, flows past executives and raw towns, and endures as "a way of happening, a mouth." Critics from Seamus Heaney to Marjorie Perloff debate whether Auden expresses disillusionment with Yeats's fascist sympathies, a broader modernist scepticism about art and action, or a paradoxical defence of poetry's marginal, therefore uncorrupted, persistence. The parish of rich women and physical decay humanise the Nobel laureate as silly like us, gift surviving folly rather than sanctifying it. Part II's longer, flowing lines prepare the tonal ascent of Part III without yet granting hymnic consolation.

> You were silly like us; your gift survived it all:  
> The parish of rich women, physical decay,  
> Yourself. Mad Ireland hurt you into poetry.  
> Now Ireland has her madness and her weather still,  
> For poetry makes nothing happen: it survives  
> In the valley of its making where executives  
> Would never want to tamper, flows on south  
> From ranches of isolation and the busy griefs,  
> Raw towns that we believe and die in; it survives,  
> A way of happening, a mouth.  
> (Auden, "In Memory of W. B. Yeats", Part II, ll. 1–11; *Another Time*, 1940)
## Earth, Receive an Honoured Guest: Nightmare Europe and the Trochaic Charge
Part III opens with burial formula and empties the vessel of its poetry before confronting the European nightmare:
The honoured guest invokes classical burial rites, yet the Irish vessel lies emptied, body and work diverge at the grave. Nightmare Europe follows with trochaic incantation:

Dogs of Europe barking, nations sequestered in hate, and pity's seas locked and frozen frame the late 1930s with unflinching political clarity. Auden then converts elegy into vocational imperative through trochaic tetrameter, a metre associated with hymn, ballad, and incantation:

"Follow, poet, follow right" charges the dead Yeats, and every successor poet, with labour at the bottom of the night. Farming a verse to make a vineyard of the curse, singing human unsuccess in rapture of distress, and teaching the free man how to praise in the prison of his days, each phrase revises Romantic triumphalism. Poetry does not abolish curse or prison; it cultivates, persuades, and instructs within them. The movement from colloquial reportage through philosophical disclaimer to trochaic hymn enacts the elegy's formal argument: art's power lies not in making events happen but in transforming how the living receive, modify, and carry forward the dead poet's words.

Controversial on publication for its qualified praise and political candour, the poem became a touchstone for debates on poetry and history. Auden later revised several lines (including excising "poetry makes nothing happen" from some readings) yet the 1940 text remains canonical. Comparative study links the elegy to Shelley's "Adonais," Milton's "Lycidas," and Heaney's Yeatsian inheritances, yet Auden's tripartite metre-shift and digestive model of influence remain distinctive.

In three parts shifting from colloquial free verse through meditative assessment to trochaic hymn, Auden conducts us from frozen brooks and deserted airports through provinces of bodily revolt, brokers on the bourse, and words modified in the guts of the living, through mad Ireland and poetry that makes nothing happen, to honoured guests, barking dogs of Europe, and the charge to teach the free man how to praise. "In Memory of W. B. Yeats" remains the definitive expression of mid-century elegiac scepticism: the claim that instruments agree on a dark cold day when a great poet dies, that gifts survive silliness and political entanglement, and that art endures as a way of happening rather than an engine of event. The poem does more than commemorate Yeats; by modulating from journalistic coldness to hymnic command, it enacts the tension between poetry's political impotence and its persistent vocation that Anglo-American literature inherits as its most quoted modern elegy.

chapters.title: 79. Pablo Neruda: Alturas de Macchu Picchu

content.value: Pablo Neruda (1904–1973)
Original title: *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*

Written 1943–1944; first published 1946 (*Rezidencia en la tierra II*); incorporated into *Canto General* (Mexico City, 1950) · Spanish · Latin American Modernism; Chilean epic lyric; postcolonial Andean poetry · Long meditative sequence in twelve cantos; free verse with incantatory repetition, apostrophe, and catalogue; postcolonial epic of ascent, archaeological encounter, and collective resurrection
## Venture into the Interior: Neruda, *Canto General*, and the Andean Ascent

Pablo Neruda's *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*—composed 1943–1944 after his 1943 journey on horseback to the ruined Inca citadel perched above the Urubamba Valley, first published in *Rezidencia en la tierra II* (1946) and later incorporated as the defining second section of *Canto General* (Mexico City, 1950)—transforms archaeological pilgrimage into postcolonial epic. The twelve-canto sequence records a symbolic "venture into the interior": ascent through loneliness, material history, and natural violence toward encounter with Macchu Picchu's stone city and its absent builders. *Canto General*, Neruda's Whitmanesque chronicle of the American continent from geological origins through conquest and revolution, gains its emotional and ideological centre from this poem's discovery of indigenous labour buried beneath imperial ruin. Robert Pring-Mill's introduction to Nathaniel Tarn's translation and Christopher Perriam's scholarship on Neruda's political poetics contextualise the work. For UGC NET English candidates tracing Latin American modernism from Modernismo through Borges and beyond, *Alturas* exemplifies how epic scale, surrealist imagery, and Marxist humanism fuse in mid-century Spanish-language poetry.

The opening cantos establish vertical movement and existential isolation. The speaker climbs through "the ladder of the kingdom of the dead," past void, thistle, and wind, shedding the "death of the world" like a worn-out skin. Early movements catalogue cosmic and geological time, salt, coal, iron, quartz, blood, before narrowing to personal loneliness:

Muddy streets and shining Sundays anchor metaphysical quest in urban mundanity before the Andean ascent strips away modern alienation. Each canto advances the climb: through rain, roots, and the "high reef of the human dawn," the poet pursues what Pring-Mill terms an interior as much as geographic journey.

> Like a lonely man I walked through the muddy streets  
> and the wet, shining Sundays.  
> (Neruda, *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*, Canto I; trans. Nathaniel Tarn; *The Heights of Macchu Picchu*, 1966)
## Twelve Cantos: From Material Labyrinth to the Stone City

The sequence's twelve-part architecture mirrors ritual ascent. Middle cantos traverse material history, factories, cemeteries, markets, and the "multitude of walls", before the poet confronts Macchu Picchu as archaeological revelation. Canto VI's famous apostrophe addresses the dead city directly:

Stone, air, and time accumulate while man remains absent, civilisation's materials outlast their makers. The citadel rises "high city of scaled stones" with ladders that end in sunlight, terraces like volcanic breakwaters, and a dwelling "like a horseshoe" cradled by mountains. Neruda's imagery fuses geological grandeur with intimate domestic scale: the city is simultaneously fortress, temple, and abandoned home. Cantos VII through XI interrogate what the stones conceal, centuries of labour, conquest, and silence, preparing the climactic address of Canto XII.

Formally, the poem employs free verse with incantatory repetition, surreal metaphors, and long Whitmanesque lines that catalogue American landscape and history. Unlike traditional European epic with heroic individual at its centre, *Alturas* distributes agency toward collective indigenous labour. The ascent structure, loneliness, material encounter, revelation, apostrophe, parallels Dante's vertical journey while replacing theological salvation with political resurrection of the oppressed.

> Stone upon stone, and man, where was he?  
> Air upon air, and man, where was he?  
> Time upon time, and man, where was he?  
> (Neruda, *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*, Canto VI; trans. Nathaniel Tarn; *The Heights of Macchu Picchu*, 1966)
## Ancient Builders: Plowman, Weaver, Shepherd, and Crushed Fingers
Before Canto XII's collective summons, Cantos X and XI recover the anonymous workers who constructed and sustained Macchu Picchu. The poet demands that the stones reveal their makers:
The buried jaguars and yellow lightning convert historical violence into sensory inundation. Neruda catalogues the ancient builders by their trades and wounds:

Plowman, weaver, shepherd, mason, water-bearer, goldsmith, farmer, potter, each figure embodies labour the tourist's gaze erases. "Mason of the impossible scaffold" and "goldsmith of crushed fingers" insist that magnificence rests on mutilated bodies. "Potter poured out into your clay" dissolves the worker into material, anticipating Canto XII's demand that the dead speak through the poet's mouth. The poem's postcolonial argument crystallises here: Macchu Picchu is both beautiful ruin and evidence of exploited craftsmanship that colonial and capitalist history has buried twice, first in earth, then in aesthetic contemplation that ignores suffering.

> Tell me everything, chain by chain,  
> link by link, and step by step.  
> Sharpen the knives you kept,  
> stick them in my breast and in my hand,  
> like a river of yellow light,  
> like a river of buried jaguars,  
> and let me weep, hours, days, years,  
> blind ages, stellar centuries.  
> (Neruda, *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*, Canto XI; trans. Mark Eisner et al.; *The Essential Neruda*, City Lights, 2004)

> Look at me from the depths of the earth,  
> plowman, weaver, silent shepherd:  
> tender of the guardian guanacos:  
> mason of the impossible scaffold:  
> water-bearer of Andean tears:  
> goldsmith of crushed fingers:  
> farmer trembling on the seed:  
> potter poured out into your clay:  
> (Neruda, *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*, Canto XII; trans. Mark Eisner et al.; *The Essential Neruda*, 2004)
## Sube a Nacer Conmigo: Whitmanesque Brotherhood and Collective Voice
Canto XII opens with the sequence's most celebrated line, converting archaeological address into fraternal resurrection:

"Sube a nacer conmigo, hermano"—Rise up and be born with me, brother, transforms elegy into nativity. The dead cannot return from rock or subterranean time; their hardened voices and drilled-out eyes remain below. Yet the poet summons them to rise through his speech, offering the cup of new life for old buried sorrows. Whitman's democratic catalogue and fraternal "I" resonate throughout: Neruda seeks to speak not for but through the oppressed, becoming vessel for silenced mouths.
The canto demands forensic testimony:

Blood, furrow, punishment, crucifixion, Christian and Marxist vocabularies merge in a tribunal of historical witness. The poet offers his chest and hand for the dead's knives, accepting their pain as medium of speech:

Speaking through dead mouths, uniting split lips, anchoring poet and labourer together, the collective voice supersedes individual lyric subjectivity. This is Neruda's answer to modernist alienation: not aesthetic autonomy but solidarity with the dispossessed.

> Rise up and be born with me, brother.  
> From the deepest reaches of your  
> disseminated sorrow, give me your hand.  
> You will not return from the depths of rock.  
> You will not return from subterranean time.  
> (Neruda, *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*, Canto XII; trans. Mark Eisner et al.; *The Essential Neruda*, 2004)

> Show me your blood and your furrow,  
> say to me: here I was punished  
> because the gem didn't shine or the earth  
> didn't deliver the stone or the grain on time:  
> point out to me the rock on which you fell  
> and the wood on which they crucified you,  
> (Neruda, *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*, Canto XII; trans. Mark Eisner et al.; *The Essential Neruda*, 2004)

> I come to speak through your dead mouth.  
> Through the earth unite all  
> the silent and split lips  
> and from the depths speak to me all night long  
> as if we were anchored together,  
> (Neruda, *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*, Canto XII; trans. Mark Eisner et al.; *The Essential Neruda*, 2004)
## Speak Through My Words and My Blood: Silence, Struggle, and Epic Closure
Canto XII closes with a series of imperative gifts that define the poet's transformed vocation:

Silence, water, and hope balance struggle, iron, and volcanoes, contemplative receptivity and revolutionary force held in tension. Bodies fastened like magnets, veins and mouth invaded by the dead: the poet's body becomes site of collective utterance. "Speak through my words and my blood" concludes the ascent by dissolving authorial ownership, Neruda's "I" is permeable, inhabited, answerable.

Within *Canto General*, *Alturas* bridges geological and pre-Columbian cantos to the conquest and liberation narratives that follow, supplying the poem with its ethical centre: the American continent's beauty is inseparable from indigenous suffering. Critics debate Neruda's romanticisation of Inca civilisation, the tension between Stalinist politics and lyrical humanism, and whether the collective voice genuinely empowers the dead or ventriloquises them. Yet the poem's influence on Latin American poetry, from Ernesto Cardenal to contemporary indigenous reclamations, remains foundational.

In twelve cantos of ascent and address, Neruda conducts us from muddy streets and cosmic materiality through stone upon stone and man-where-was-he, through plowmen and goldsmiths of crushed fingers, to rise up and be born with me, brother, and speak through my words and my blood. *Alturas de Macchu Picchu* remains the definitive expression of postcolonial epic lyric: the claim that archaeological splendour must be read as monument to anonymous labour, that the poet's vocation is to speak through dead mouths rather than over them, and that brotherhood means resurrection in language rather than return from subterranean time. The poem does more than describe Macchu Picchu; by climbing from loneliness to collective apostrophe, it enacts the Whitmanesque expansion of voice that *Canto General* and twentieth-century Latin American literature inherit as their most impassioned statement of poetic solidarity.
**Word count (body):** 1,512

> Give me silence, water, hope.  
> Give me struggle, iron, volcanoes.  
> Fasten your bodies to mine like magnets.  
> Come to my veins and to my mouth.  
> Speak through my words and my blood.  
> (Neruda, *Alturas de Macchu Picchu*, Canto XII; trans. Mark Eisner et al.; *The Essential Neruda*, 2004)
Dylan Thomas (1914–1953)
Original title: "Fern Hill"

Written 1945; first published 1946 · English (Welsh English inflection) · Welsh Modernism; Anglo-Welsh lyric; post-Romantic pastoral elegy · Meditative pastoral lyric in nine stanzas of syllabic verse (approximately nine lines per stanza with intricate internal rhyme and assonance); recollection of childhood innocence and time's betrayal
## Young and Easy: Welsh Farm Childhood and Edenic Innocence

Dylan Thomas's "Fern Hill"—written in 1945 at the Blaen Cwm cottage in Carmarthenshire and first published in *Deaths and Entrances* (Dent, 1946)—recreates the poet's childhood summers at his aunt Ann Jones's farm near Llangain, transforming autobiographical pasture into mythic Eden before time's fall. Composed as Thomas emerged from the Second World War's shadow, the poem belongs to the collection's broader meditation on innocence, mortality, and entrance into adult consciousness. Fern Hill itself was the farmland's name; Thomas's radio broadcast "Reminiscences of Childhood" and Constantine FitzGibbon's biography anchor the pastoral in documented Welsh landscape. Paul Ferris's *Dylan Thomas: The Biography* and Walford Davies's commentary on Thomas's syllabic craft contextualise the poem's formal achievement. For UGC NET English candidates tracing twentieth-century pastoral from Wordsworth and Hopkins to Heaney, "Fern Hill" exemplifies how Welsh English lyric fuses child's perception, biblical myth, and intricate sound-patterning into a definitive statement on lost innocence.
The opening stanza establishes the child's sovereign ease beneath apple boughs:

Young and easy under apple boughs, happy as the grass was green, the child inhabits a world where night is starry above the dingle and time permits hailing and climbing. "Once below a time" inverts fairy-tale formula ("once upon a time") into vertical pastoral geography, below time, beneath history's pressure. Prince of the apple towns and lordly among trees, the child possesses prelapsarian sovereignty without labour. Windfall light rivers through daisies and barley, converting harvest surplus into luminous play. The stanza's syllabic lines, approximately nine per stanza with shifting indentations, create incantatory rhythm that suspends chronological urgency.

> Now as I was young and easy under the apple boughs  
> About the lilting house and happy as the grass was green,  
> The night above the dingle starry,  
> Time let me hail and climb  
> Golden in the heydays of his eyes,  
> And honoured among wagons I was prince of the apple towns  
> And once below a time I lordly had the trees and leaves  
> Trail with daisies and barley  
> Down the rivers of the windfall light.  
> (Thomas, "Fern Hill", stanza I; *Deaths and Entrances*, 1946)
## Time Let Me Play: Personification and the Mercy of His Means
Stanza II intensifies the personification of Time as benevolent patron:

Green and carefree, famous among barns, the child sings as the farm becomes home. "The sun that is young once only" introduces transience through negation, the sun's youthfulness is unrepeatable, though the child has not yet recognised the condition. Time lets him play and be golden in the mercy of his means: Time possesses means (agricultural seasons, daylight, growth) and grants them mercifully. Huntsman and herdsman, the child joins a pastoral economy where calves sing to his horn and foxes bark on hills. Sabbath ringing slowly in pebbles of holy streams fuses Welsh chapel culture with natural sacrament. Thomas's Welsh upbringing, English verse inflected by Carmarthenshire speech rhythms, grounds the mythic in regional particularity.

> And as I was green and carefree, famous among the barns  
> About the happy yard and singing as the farm was home,  
> In the sun that is young once only,  
> Time let me play and be  
> Golden in the mercy of his means,  
> And green and golden I was huntsman and herdsman, the calves  
> Sang to my horn, the foxes on the hills barked clear and cold,  
> And the sabbath rang slowly  
> In the pebbles of the holy streams.  
> (Thomas, "Fern Hill", stanza II; *Deaths and Entrances*, 1946)
## Running, Lovely, Watery: Hayfields, Owls, and the Farm Borne Away
Stanzas III and IV expand the day's sensory abundance and the dreamlike passage into sleep:

Hayfields high as the house, chimney tunes, air and playing, loveliness and wateriness, fire green as grass, the catalogue converts farm labour into child's play through adjectival accumulation. Riding to sleep under simple stars, the child experiences dream-logic: owls bear the farm away, nightjars fly with ricks, horses flash into dark. Sleep is voyage; the farm becomes mobile, released from gravity. Stanza IV's awakening restores the Edenic garden:

Adam and maiden, birth of simple light, first spinning place, fields of praise, Thomas explicitly biblicalises the farm. Each morning re-enacts creation; the sun grows round that very day as if newly minted. Spellbound horses walking warm from whinnying green stable into fields of praise convert agricultural routine into liturgical procession. Innocence here is not ignorance but fullness of presence: the child inhabits each dawn as inaugural.

> All the sun long it was running, it was lovely, the hay  
> Fields high as the house, the tunes from the chimneys, it was air  
> And playing, lovely and watery  
> And fire green as grass.  
> And nightly under the simple stars  
> As I rode to sleep the owls were bearing the farm away,  
> All the moon long I heard, blessed among stables, the nightjars  
> Flying with the ricks, and the horses  
> Flashing into the dark.  
> (Thomas, "Fern Hill", stanza III; *Deaths and Entrances*, 1946)

> And then to awake, and the farm, like a wanderer white  
> With the dew, come back, the cock on his shoulder: it was all  
> Shining, it was Adam and maiden,  
> The sky gathered again  
> And the sun grew round that very day.  
> So it must have been after the birth of the simple light  
> In the first, spinning place, the spellbound horses walking warm  
> Out of the whinnying green stable  
> On to the fields of praise.  
> (Thomas, "Fern Hill", stanza IV; *Deaths and Entrances*, 1946)
## Heedless Ways: Creation Myth and the Foreshadowing of Loss
Stanzas V through VII maintain golden abundance while introducing subtle foreshadowing:

Heedless ways and sky blue trades measure innocence as economic and imaginative freedom, the child trades in sky, not currency. Yet "time allows / In all his tuneful turning so few and such morning songs / Before the children green and golden / Follow him out of grace" introduces the fall before narrating it. Children follow time out of grace as he turns tunefully onward; the syntax anticipates betrayal within celebration. Thomas's intricate rhyme, often internal and slant, binds stanzas acoustically while meaning drifts toward loss. The farm's gay house, new-made clouds, and sun born over and over sustain Edenic recurrence, but the poem's structure prepares rupture.

> And honoured among foxes and pheasants by the gay house  
> Under the new made clouds and happy as the heart was long,  
> In the sun born over and over,  
> I ran my heedless ways,  
> My wishes raced through the house high hay  
> And nothing I cared, at my sky blue trades, that time allows  
> In all his tuneful turning so few and such morning songs  
> Before the children green and golden  
> Follow him out of grace,  
> (Thomas, "Fern Hill", stanza V; *Deaths and Entrances*, 1946)
## Green and Dying: Chains, the Sea, and Time's Realisation
The final stanzas enact the fall from unclouded childhood into consciousness of mortality:

Lamb white days yield to time's capture: the swallow-thronged loft, the shadow of the hand, the moon always rising, these emblems register growing self-consciousness. Riding to sleep, the child hears time fly with the high fields; waking, the farm is forever fled from the childless land. Adulthood is childless land from which the farm has departed, not because the farm vanished but because the child's access to it is irrevocably lost. The closing lines deliver the poem's central paradox:

Time holds the child green and dying simultaneously, life and mortality inseparable in retrospect. Chains suggest temporal bondage, yet the child sings like the sea: movement within constraint, music within limit. The simile transforms chains from pure oppression into rhythmic endurance. Innocence is not ignorance of death but blissful postponement of its recognition; the adult speaker recreates what time has stolen, singing in chains as the poem itself becomes the farm's resurrection in language.

"Fern Hill" influenced subsequent pastoral elegy from Seamus Heaney's Irish farms to contemporary memoir poetry. Thomas's syllabic stanzas, neither strict metre nor free verse, create hypnotic recurrence that enacts time's circular generosity before linear loss. Critics note the poem's debt to Blake's innocence, Wordsworth's *Intimations* Ode, and Hopkins's sprung rhythm while insisting on Thomas's acoustic originality.

In nine syllabic stanzas, Thomas conducts us from young and easy apple boughs and prince of the apple towns through time let me play and golden mercy, through hayfields high as the house and Adam and maiden mornings, through heedless ways and sun born over and over, to time held me green and dying though I sang in my chains like the sea. "Fern Hill" remains the definitive expression of Edenic childhood recollected after loss: the claim that once below a time the farm was shining creation, that time's mercy permits play before grace is forfeited, and that the adult poet's song transforms chains into sea-like endurance. The poem does more than describe Welsh farm summers; by moving from lilting house to farm forever fled from the childless land, it enacts the realisation that innocence and mortality were always intertwined, and that art's vocation is to sing within that double bind.
**Word count (body):** 1,627

> Nothing I cared, in the lamb white days, that time would take me  
> Up to the swallow thronged loft by the shadow of my hand,  
> In the moon that is always rising,  
> Nor that riding to sleep  
> I should hear him fly with the high fields  
> And wake to the farm forever fled from the childless land.  
> Oh as I was young and easy in the mercy of his means,  
> Time held me green and dying  
> Though I sang in my chains like the sea.  
> (Thomas, "Fern Hill", stanzas VIII–IX; *Deaths and Entrances*, 1946)

> Time held me green and dying  
> Though I sang in my chains like the sea.  
> (Thomas, "Fern Hill", stanza IX, ll. 8–9; *Deaths and Entrances*, 1946)
Paul Celan (Paul Antschel, 1920–1970)
Original title: "Todesfuge"

Written 1944–1945; first published 1948 (*Aufbau*, Berlin) · German (with biblical and musical allusion) · Post-Holocaust European lyric; Romanian-born German-language poetry; transnational witness writing after Auschwitz · Fugue-structured elegy in irregular stanzas with refrain and counter-subject; concentration-camp allegory in musical form
## Schwarze Milch der Frühe: Buchenwald, the Fugue, and Poetry After Auschwitz

Paul Celan's "Todesfuge"—composed in Bucharest between 1944 and 1945, after the poet's return from forced labour and news of his parents' deportation and murder, and first published in the journal *Aufbau* (Berlin, 1948)—is the most widely debated German-language poem of the Holocaust. Celan, born Paul Antschel in Czernowitz (then Romania, now Ukraine), survived the Shoah while his mother was shot and his father died of typhus; the poem's camp imagery draws on reports from Transnistria and the extermination centres without naming a specific site, converting historical atrocity into a musical nightmare. The title announces death (*Tod*) in fugue (*Fuge*) form: voices enter, repeat, and interweave according to contrapuntal rules that the poem simultaneously obeys and violates. John Felstiner's *Paul Celan: Poet, Survivor, Jew* and Pierre Joris's translations anchor Anglophone study; Theodor W. Adorno's dictum that "to write poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric" (*Prisms*, 1955) frames nearly every reading of the text, though Celan's defenders argue that the poem does not aestheticise horror so much as expose the impossibility of adequate language. For UGC NET English candidates tracing post-war European poetry, Holocaust testimony, and the ethics of representation, "Todesfuge" demands analysis of how musical structure, mythic allusion, and repetition enact complicity and witness at once.
The opening line fuses nourishment and poison, morning and extinction:

Black milk of morning, they drink it evenings, middays, mornings, nights; they drink and drink. The oxymoron annihilates pastoral and maternal imagery: milk should be white, morning should nourish, yet both are black and compulsively consumed. Felstiner notes the echo of Nietzsche's "black milk of daybreak" in an earlier Celan draft; here the phrase becomes refrain, returning like a cantus firmus through each stanza. Drinking schedules (evenings, middays, mornings, nights) suggest ritual without sacrament, perpetual ingestion of what kills. The poem's German enacts what Celan later called the "thousand darknesses of deathbringing speech": grammar holds while meaning corrodes.

> Schwarze Milch der Frühe wir trinken sie abends  
> wir trinken sie mittags und morgens wir trinken sie nachts  
> wir trinken und trinken  
> (Celan, "Todesfuge", opening stanza; *Aufbau*, 1948)
## Der Tod ist ein Meister aus Deutschland: Death, the Camp Commandant, and National Complicity
The poem's most quoted refrain personifies death as German master:

Death is a master from Germany; his eye is blue; he strikes you with leaden bullet, strikes you true. The blue eye conflates Aryan racial ideology with the camp officer's gaze; mastery belongs to Germany as a nation, extending beyond individual perpetrators. "Leaden bullet" and precision ("genau") suggest industrial execution, shooting as craft. The refrain alternates with passages of music and labour:

Death plays with his henchmen, writes a birthday on the wall, and plays death, the death is a master from Germany. Birthday on the wall recalls prison graffiti and arbitrary cruelty; play and writing convert murder into game. Celan's diction refuses the consolations of elegy: no redemption, no heroism, only mechanical recurrence.

> Der Tod ist ein Meister aus Deutschland sein Auge ist blau  
> er trifft dich mit bleierner Kugel er trifft dich genau  
> (Celan, "Todesfuge", refrain; *Aufbau*, 1948)

> er spielt mit den Schergen er schreibt ein Geburtstag an die Wand  
> und spielt den Tod den Tod ist ein Meister aus Deutschland  
> (Celan, "Todesfuge"; *Aufbau*, 1948)
## Margarete und Shulamith: Goethe, the Bible, and Hair as Counter-Subject
The fugue's counter-subject pairs two women whose names carry entire literary and scriptural histories:

Your golden hair Margarete; your ashen hair Shulamith. Margarete invokes Goethe's *Faust*—golden-haired Gretchen, emblem of German Romantic lyric and innocent femininity. Shulamith names the beloved in the Song of Songs, here reduced to ash. The poem weaves their names through stanzas as hair transforms from gold to ash:

He calls: strike deeper into the earth, you still let gleam in your ash-pit; he calls: play sweeter, death. Golden hair and ashen hair become fugue subjects that cannot harmonise: German cultural inheritance (Goethe, music, blue-eyed mastery) proceeds alongside Jewish annihilation. Critics including Felstiner read Margarete as the Aryan ideal implicated in Shulamith's destruction; others stress that both names are spoken by the same collective "we," collapsing witness and victim into one unbearable voice.

> dein goldenes Haar Margarete  
> dein aschenes Haar Shulamith  
> (Celan, "Todesfuge"; *Aufbau*, 1948)

> er ruft stecht tiefer ins Erz ihr laßt euch noch Glanz in eurem Ascheloch  
> er ruft spielt süßer den Tod der Tod ist ein Meister aus Deutschland  
> (Celan, "Todesfuge"; *Aufbau*, 1948)
## Musik der Vergangenheit und Schläge aufs Geigen: Bach, SS Culture, and the Dance of the Dead
Musical imagery saturates the camp scene:
Death wears a poppy from Germany, opium flower, remembrance emblem, blood-red decoration. Earlier stanzas command sweeter playing, deeper digging, and invoke violins and graves:

They shovel a grave in the air where one does not lie cramped, a direct echo of concentration-camp labour turned surreal. Bach's fugues, German high culture, and SS officers who reportedly enjoyed classical music furnish the poem's bitter counterpoint: civilisation and extermination share a language of mastery and sweetness. The "we" who drink black milk and shovel aerial graves may be prisoners, corpses, or a fractured collective conscience; Celan withholds stable identity, forcing readers to inhabit complicity without resolution.

> er ruft spielt süßer den Tod der Tod ist ein Meister aus Deutschland  
> der Tod trägt eine Mohnblume aus Deutschland  
> (Celan, "Todesfuge"; *Aufbau*, 1948)

> Schwarze Milch der Frühe wir trinken dich mittags  
> der Tod ist ein Meister aus Deutschland  
> wir schaufeln ein Grab in den Lüften da liegt man nicht eng  
> (Celan, "Todesfuge"; *Aufbau*, 1948)
## Adorno, Celan, and the Ethics of the Survivor's Lyric

Adorno's statement that poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric has been misread as prohibition; in context, Adorno criticises culture that proceeds unchanged after catastrophe. Celan's poem answers by making barbarism visible within lyric form, death as master, black milk, ash hair, without claiming to heal. The fugue structure implies order (subject, answer, stretto) yet the content annihilates that order: music accompanies shooting, birthdays are written on walls, graves are dug in sky. When Celan read "Todesfuge" publicly, audiences reportedly wept; when he grew older, he reportedly distanced himself from the poem's fame, fearing it had become aesthetic monument rather than wound.

Influential across Holocaust literature and musicology, "Todesfuge" shaped debates on whether art can represent genocide. Translations by Felstiner, Joris, and Michael Hamburger carry the refrain's terrible clarity into English classrooms; Germanists note Celan's neologisms and compressed syntax as resistance to fluent narrative. The poem does not document a single transport or barrack; it compresses the camp into perpetual present tense, always drinking, always playing, always striking true.

Each subsequent line ends similarly with "We," forcing breath pause before the next verb phrase begins. Brooks's form lesson, ending each line with "We", teaches how layout shapes meaning. Printed poem resembles pool table rectangle; couplets suggest paired players or mirrored shots. Reading aloud, audience participates in syncopation: "We real cool. \[pause\] We left school." The pause is where cool lives, in hesitation before next risk. Compared to Ginsberg's expansive *Howl* or Plath's theatrical tercets, Brooks's miniature proves that scale does not limit scope.

Influence extends through spoken-word pedagogy and anthologies; the poem is among America's most taught lyrics, sometimes reduced to slogan. Brooks resisted simplification: light reading carries heavy prophecy. Sound devices, monosyllables, internal rhyme, anaphoric "We", create memorable chant; semantic darkness waits in final two words. In eight coupleted lines and seven terminal "We"s, Brooks conducts us from real cool and left school through lurk late and strike straight, through sing sin and thin gin, to jazz June and die soon. > Or, after dark, will dubious women come  
> To make their children touch a particular stone;  
> Pick simples for a cancer; or on some  
> Advised night see walking a dead one?  
> (Larkin, "Church Going", stanza V; *The Less Deceived*, 1955)

> Power of some sort or other will go on  
> In games, in riddles, seemingly at random;  
> But superstition, like belief, must die,  
> And what remains when disbelief has gone?  
> Grass, weedy pavement, brambles, buttress, sky,  
> A shape less recognizable each week,  
> A purpose more obscure. I wonder who  
> Will be the last, the very last, to seek  
> This place for what it was; one of the crew  
> That tap and jot and know what rood-lofts were?  
> (Larkin, "Church Going", stanza VI; *The Less Deceived*, 1955)
## Death and Destiny: The Unrobing, Unbribable Priest
The final stanza delivers the poem's most solemn projection, a future worshiper and the church's ultimate destiny:

Some ruin-bibber randy for antique, Christmas-addict craving gown-and-bands, or will he be the speaker's representative, bored and uninformed, knowing ghostly silt dispersed yet tending this cross of ground through suburb scrub because it held unspilt so long what since is found only in separation: marriage, birth, death, and thoughts of these. Though the accoutred frowsty barn's worth is unknown, standing in silence pleases, the final admission that scepticism has not extinguished appetite for consecrated pause. Critics from Barbara Everett to Terry Eagleton debate whether Larkin's conclusion affirms human seriousness or merely documents its nostalgia; the poem's form enacts the tension through colloquial opening modulating into elevated repetition of stanza IV's central lines.

"Church Going" influenced Heaney's sacred sites, Douglas Dunn's parish poems, and contemporary British poets who treat churches as secular heritage. Compared to Gray's *Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard*, Larkin interiorises pilgrimage, the speaker enters the building rather than contemplating externals, and replaces mute inglorious Miltons with bicycle clips and Irish sixpences. Compared to Arnold's "Dover Beach," Larkin locates residual seriousness in architecture and rite rather than in love's remaining shore.

In seven nine-line stanzas, Larkin conducts us from cycle-clips and awkward reverence through matting, seats, and stone, through hectoring verses and Irish sixpences, through a serious house on serious earth where compulsions meet robed as destinies, through churches fallen out of use and dubious women touching stones, through power that continues in games and riddles, to the bored representative tending cross of ground where marriage, birth, and death remain found only in separation. "Church Going" remains the definitive expression of post-war English religious scepticism that cannot abandon sacred architecture: the claim that someone will forever surprise a hunger to be more serious and gravitate to ground proper for growing wise among the dead, that churches robe compulsions as destinies even when belief has departed, and that an accoutred frowsty barn pleases the agnostic who stands in silence because so many dead lie round. The poem does more than describe an empty parish church; by moving from comic cycle-clips to solemn meditation on what survives when superstition and belief have died, it enacts the very hunger for seriousness it diagnoses, a Movement landmark that proves realism can ascend without ceasing to be conversational.
